speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (for the Minister of Finance) moved
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
that Bill C-143, to provide supplementary borrowing authority, be read the third time and do pass.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I want to conclude my comments on this legislation by addressing three areas under the following headings: Why is the Government requesting authority to borrow at this time? What will the money be used for? How does the Government control these expenditures, and indeed expenditures generally?
I remind Hon. Members of the financial statement of October 27 by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) wherein he made the following comments:
I have also made it clear from the estimates I have presented that further borrowing authority will be required before the end of this fiscal year. In the budget I intend to present early in 1983, I will review again the fiscal situation for the current fiscal year, set out estimates for 1983-1984 and future fiscal years, and then seek additional borrowing authority as required.
The Minister of Finance has indicated that he will set the date for the upcoming budget within the next few days. Addressing the first part of the Bill, in the interim and, second, in the immediate period of the budget and post-budget, interim borrowing authority is sought. That is the purpose of the legislation before us.
What about the funds which are sought under this request for authority to borrow? We know that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) tabled in this House some 6,000 pages of Main Estimates. This is an indication of the expenditure program of the Government, which is an annual event for programs established under authority of legislation of Parliament. In tabling the estimates, the President of the Treasury Board signalled that two-thirds of these budgetary estimates are slated for statutory expenditures based on continuing authority by Acts of Parliament. These estimates show in great detail the wide variety of programs being carried out by the Government, living up to its responsibilities under the legislation I have just indicated, and assisting Canadians during this very significant downturn in the economy.
The estimates reflect a 21 per cent rise in cash payments under the Established Programs Financing Act whereby the
federal Government contributes to the financing of hospital insurance, medicare, extended health care and post-secondary education. They indicate a $2.9 billion allocation to Unemployment Insurance in order to assist in this recessionary time in the economy. The estimates demonstrate a 21 per cent increase in federal contributions to the Provinces, for example, and to the Canada Assistance Plan.
The federal Government pays for 50 per cent of eligible provincial-municipal expenditures for assistance payments, welfare payments and a number of health programs. We also cover 50 per cent of the cost of child support services such as foster care, daycare, and a broad array of family and social support services. I do not have to remind Hon. Members of the continuing and pressing need for funding in this area. That is what the Government intends to address through the funds sought by the authority in the legislation before us today.
More than that, scarcely a day goes by, Mr. Speaker, but that we are reminded of the initiatives taken by the Government, again signalled in the October 27 statement of the Minister of Finance, for example through the NEED Program, job-generation programs which are designed to assist people whose Unemployment Insurance benefits are terminating. The funding for that program is assisted by the request for authority presently before the House and in the legislation for which we seek approval today.
With respect to the comments which have been made that the expenditures are not wisely or efficiently accounted for- and this is the third point I wish to draw to the attention of Hon. Members-I remind them again that this Government accepted the recommendations of the Royal Commission on Financial Management and Accountability, the Lambert Commission. This Government, together with the former Conservative Government, has accepted the procedure whereby expenditures of the Government are split, in terms of Cabinet responsibilities, into a number of envelopes. Within these envelopes, Ministers of kin responsibilities are obliged to set priorities and to set off against one another claims for expenditures in their areas of responsibility.
There are other controls as well, Mr. Speaker. All budgetary appropriations of funds, of course, must be approved by Parliament, and we have the system of a very detailed examination of the estimates through the Standing Committees of the House. For example, on two occasions I have been before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs to account for, explain and give detailed responses to

March 29, 1983
Borrowing Authority
detailed questions of Eton. Members as to the expenditure in the Department of Insurance. Therefore, each Minister of the Government is called before Standing Committees of the House to answer and to account for the expenditures of the Government, not only for the funds which are sought today in this legislation, but all other operations of the Government.
We know as well, Mr. Speaker, some of us only too dearly, that Treasury Board is a mechanism of the Government, this Government and the preceding Conservative Government, which guards jealously the actual implementation and expenditure of funds under general programs. We know as well that the Auditor General examines the Government's financial statements and carefully reports to Parliament on his findings. I would like to repeat again what I said earlier in our deliberations on this legislation, that so much good work was done by the former Auditor General, Mr. Macdonell. He showed such leadership in strengthening the controls and the overview of Government expenditures in that part of Government operations through the exercise of the office of the Auditor General.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, in a broader policy range, in 1975 the Government announced that it would hold the trend growth of its expenditures to no more than the general trend growth of the economy. I remind Hon. Members that over the period from 1975 to 1980 the Government successfully met that objective. In 1981, of course, with the deterioration of the economy, expenditures rose more rapidly and that was witnessed by the Government's response, for example, in increasing its commitment to Unemployment Insurance payments and, unfortunately, as well, calling for a similar increase in contributions by the private sector in order to meet a situation which, as I have indicated, was caused by the downturn in the economy.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I have attempted very briefly, under three headings, to address what I believe to be three important points that Hon. Members will take into account when considering the request by the Government for the borrowing authority in the legislation before us this morning.
I have attempted to explain, first, that the Government requires this authority to meet pressing needs of Canadians. That, I think, in normal times would have been explanation enough; it is to meet the ongoing expenditures of the Government particularly at this time of year.
Second, I have indicated that the Government through the estimates, in thousands and thousands of items, has detailed the expenditures.
Finally, I have attempted to outline the controls and safeguards that guide the Government in its attempt, efficiently and in a businesslike way, to manage the expenditure of funds, not only in this authority to borrow but in all Government expenditures. I urge Hon. Members to conclude this debate and to vote, enabling the Government to proceed with this authority as quickly as possible.

speakeroldname: Hon. Erik Nielsen (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there can be no doubt that the Government has so mismanaged the economy of the country that it is now broke. It is utterly broke. It has exercised emergency powers under Section 39 of the Financial Administration Act for the first time in our history.
Last Friday when I raised the matter with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) in the House, he tried to draw a parallel between what he was doing in exercising the powers granted to him under Section 39 of the Financial Administration Act and circumstances which occurred in 1962. There is no relationship whatsoever. This is the first time in our history that the Government has gone to emergency borrowing powers, once a week, and has borrowed in excess of $2.5 billion according to orders in council tabled in the House yesterday. That is a shameful situation, Mr. Speaker.
We find statements of the Minister of Finance such as those which appeared in The Globe and Mail recently, when he said that the federal Government deficit is like an accordion, to be a very curious view of the deficit. He should learn to play better than he sings. In his hands the deficit has been more like a balloon which is constantly being inflated by the Government and which, at some point, must burst.
The Minister's role as an accordion player is very appropriate. It conjures up the image of the organ grinder. And what does that make the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove)? Is he the one who carries the tin cup? The problem between the Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Finance is that it is difficult to know, from time to time, who is playing and who is dancing. I can tell the Minister of State for Finance where the majority of Canadians would like to see him and his colleagues on the Treasury benches these days, and it is not where they presently are.
We confront this Bill among gathering clouds of uncertainty and the highest unemployment rate since the great Depression. It is in this context that the Government seeks authority to borrow $19 billion to meet its cash requirements, in the meantime exercising emergency powers to stay afloat. As has been pointed out time after time in the House, of the total amount, $14 billion relates to the coming fiscal year, to budgetary demands, to fiscal and monetary policies of which the House has not yet been given an inkling. We are being asked to finance policies that we have not yet seen and to underwrite programs which we know nothing about.
The most serious issue in this country today, sir, is the two million Canadians who cannot find jobs. Another 600,000 students and young people are coming on to the labour market in the next month or two with no hope that there is going to be employment in this land which used to be a land of plenty before these rascals did it in. There is no indication, sir, that this Bill will in any way address the problems of those two million unemployed Canadians and the 600,000 young people coming on to the job market this summer. This Government, sir, has shown itself to be totally unconcerned about the
March 29, 1983

unemployed. It has taken an utterly cavalier attitude towards unemployment.
This, sir, is the Government that turned off the tap, that froze out foreign investment, that obstructed the oil and gas industry, that fumbled the megaprojects. This is the Government that accorded special treatment to its friends. It put one former assistant of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) at the head of the Canada Development Investment Corporation with powers of life and death over a multitude of companies and corporations, and another Minister to whom the first must report. The Prime Minister showed his concern for the unemployed when he relegated the discussions on the economy to a dinnertime chat with the Premiers and then put it back to the evening prior to the opening of the constitutional meeting in mid-March. He had an in depth discussion of the unemployment problem in this country, an in depth discussion of the serious economic problems facing the country, and in depth, detailed discussion between the vichyssoise and the filet mignon. To hundreds of thousands of unemployed Canadians, the signal is clear: beware the Ides of March. That, sir, is not good enough.
The Conservative Party, in the face of the enveloping crisis rending this country on the jobless issue, would call a national conference lasting from two to three days and bring in the Premiers with representatives of business and industry to organize a concerted attack on the problem of unemployment. The Minister has said he needs the borrowing Bill to pay Unemployment Insurance claims which are speculated to be in the order of $12 billion and to pay welfare and create jobs. If the Government had not turned off jobs in the first place with negative and destructive policies like FIRA and the NEP, we would not have these enormous cash requirements.

speechtext: I join the millions of Canadians who say that this Government is doing a rotten job, and the sooner they get off those Treasury benches, the better.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
The Minister knows very well that one of the major reasons for this unusual demand of $14 billion in the coming fiscal year is to service the huge borrowing already undertaken by this Government. Sir, they are borrowing to pay their debts. The Government's debt charges now represent nearly a fifth of all its expenditures. When a Government reaches that point, insolvency is no longer just a word. I emphasize again that the Government's cash requirements in the coming fiscal year should be outlined in budgetary form. That is the practice of this place; that is the tradition of this place; that is the history of this place.
[DOT] (U30)
This Bill should be accompanied by a budget in which the Government sets out the specific purposes of the expenditures, the reasons for these huge cash requirements, and outlines the fiscal and monetary positions which it intends to take in order to restore the country's economy. A few moments ago the Minister of State for Finance was lauding the Committee system and the number of times that he and other Ministers appeared before Committees to examine these expenditures. I see him nodding his head in the affirmative. What time do Members of Parliament get in this great Committee system to question in detail about expenditures of this nature? Five minutes for $14 billion!

Then Members, like that yappy one over there, dragged red herrings throughout the whole process of the Committee system, taking up time and making excuses for a Government which does not know where it is going or where it has been.
The House and the country are also entitled, as a concomitant of this Bill, to an outline of the taxation policies which the Government intends to impose in order to raise funds to meet these pyramiding debt charges. That is why we need a budget. The country is entitled to know where we are going. The reason we do not know where we are going is that the Government does not know where it is going. This House is entitled to have full information and we get the least.
The reason the Government has not seen fit to fill in the budgetary blanks in its fiscal and monetary position is very simple. The Government cannot tell the House where it is going because it does not have the least idea. There is another reason that it does not tell us. It is because it does not want Canadians to know the deep trouble into which it has plunged the country. It is quite obvious that the Government, in coming here with its hand out for a blank cheque covering the coming fiscal period, without the usual explanations and with no true

indication of the present state of the economy, is desperately trying to keep from Canadians the raw truth about the serious difficulties in which we find ourselves.
We are entitled to a full budgetary background to this Bill. We do not have it because the Government does not dare to give it. To do so would be to let the cat of fiscal mismanagement out of the bag. The Government does not dare let Canadians know how close to the edge of economic insolvency it is now hovering.
The Minister talks glibly of letting the deficit grow and of spending to stimulate the economy. This is another example of that peculiar irresponsibility by which Members of the Government are afflicted. How could any Government in this country spend more than this Government has spent? They are heading for total expenditures, I believe, of $90 billion. How could they possibly make the deficit any larger? If anyone could accomplish it, they are the gang who can. It is now moving up to $30 billion. If there was any way of stimulating the economy, would it not have been stimulated by the enormous expenditures of the Government? The economy is certainly not suffering from understimulation: it is suffering from raw, bad management. It is suffering from waste, extravagance, lack of direction, confusion and the application of ideological nostrums to our economic problems.
Without exception, every policy application by the Government in the past three years has had a negative impact. Another wave of reckless spending by the denizens of the Langevin Block will not restore investor confidence one iota. A further demoralization of our fiscal standing will not bring back the megaprojects. The only cure for the condition in which the country finds itself is the removal of this Government and a return to coherent, practical policies directed to the realitites of our economy, which those fellows just choose not to recognize.
Turning to just one area of the Government's stumble-footed approach to the economy, let me point out that in the United States oil companies in the private sector pay substantial fees into the federal treasury for the privilege of undertaking exploration. In this country continuing Government interference has destroyed the confidence of entrepreneurs to the point where those who have not pulled up stakes are now being paid incentives by the Government to undertake exploration. What a topsy-turvy fiscal policy!
This is not a sign of lack of confidence in Canada; this is a sign of a total lack of confidence in the Government. It is clear that foreign investment will not come into the Beaufort Sea, to give one example, in the very large amounts necessary as long as the Government's centralist and interventionist policies continue to operate. Therein lies the tragedy of our situation. That is why unemployment is at an all time high. All this is spite of the fact that expenditures have increased under the Government since 1968-79 by some 630 per cent.
Then you ask, sir, where are the jobs? Where are the jobs that should have resulted from this enormous stimulation of the economy? The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) will tell you, sir, of the thousands and thousands of jobs he has created, paper jobs. The Minister of
Finance will talk of the billions he has poured into job creation. Where are the jobs which have resulted from these enormous expenditures? If they had created one-tenth of the jobs they claim, there would not be a single unemployed person in the country.
It is the duty of the House to vote down this Bill until such time as Parliament has full information. Certainly we in the Official Opposition intend to do just that. To do otherwise is an insult to nearly two million unemployed Canadians and a smack in the face for 600,000 young people coming on to the job market this summer.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not pleased to rise today to speak during time allocation on a Bill which asks Parliament to approve the borrowing of $19 billion. In fact, $19 billion is the largest borrowing authority the House of Commons has ever witnessed. We are debating this matter today under time allocation, which is a euphemism for closure, for muzzling Parliament, for cutting off debate and for stopping the Opposition from raising critical points. That is what closure or time allocation is all about.
We are seeing a Government which says that it can no longer take the heat, that it can no longer stand the points raised by Opposition Members; so it muzzles the Opposition and makes a mockery out of the House of Commons. The people of this country have felt very strongly about this institution of the House of Commons. We have come to respect the Mother of Parliament in the United Kingdom and Canadians have respected the House of Commons for many generations. Recently, however, the Government of Canada has made a mockery of the House of Commons.
The role of Parliament is to collect taxes wisely and spend them wisely. We have just witnessed the spectacle of Bill C-139 being introduced in the House. Once again, Parliament was muzzled and debate terminated by the Government's closure motion because the Opposition was criticizing the tax system. We said that we did not believe that 139 changes in tax legislation were appropriate at this time and that grabbing more taxes was not an appropriate step. We said that we did not believe that raising taxes for low and middle income Canadians in this country while giving tax breaks to the rich was the approach to take. We were speaking against that Bill until the Government muzzled us in Parliament and eliminated our criticisms by its closure motion.
Today we are once again asked enthusiastically to endorse the borrowing of $19 billion without knowing precisely how the money will be spent. I suggest that if any individual Canadian or Member of Parliament were to go to a bank, credit union or caisse populaire and ask the manager for $2,000, $20,000 or $200,000, we would then be expected to explain how we would use that money. That is not an unreasonable request. A prudent bank manager would expect to be told how that money would be used and repaid.
March 29, 1983

That is all that Members of the Opposition are asking the Government. We simply want to know how it will use the $19 billion because past experience does not give us much confidence in simply writing the Government a blank cheque. However, many Members on the Government side have stood up to say that they will not tell us how the money will be spent. They either do not know or have any faith in what they will do, but they will not tell us. It is unrealistic for the Government of Canada to ask us, as concerned Members of Parliament, to endorse a borrowing authority of $19 billion without illustrating very clearly how that money will be used.
Two million people have lost their jobs in this country. Many of those jobs will not be reinstated when the recovery eventually occurs. As well, there are hundreds of thousands of Canadians living daily under the threat of job loss and wondering whether they will be receiving termination or lay-off notices at the end of each week or whether they will be cut back to three or four working days a week. An increasing proportion of our population live in an atmosphere of uncertainty and fear.
One of the most disgraceful acts that I have recently witnessed occurred when the chief financial adviser to the Government, the Governor of the Bank of Canada, Gerald Bouey, said that the question asked by the two million unemployed Canadians and the some 600,000 young Canadians who will be graduating from vocational schools, universities and colleges without prospects of employment about what the Government will do about unemployment was the wrong question. His response was that the question should not concern what the Government will do about it or how it will put these people back to work but how soon will the inflation rate be reduced.
Can you imagine anything more ridiculous in your life than to go to an unemployed person who has worked for many years of his or her life in a plant, factory, office or shop, only to find themselves unemployed through no fault of their own and with likely no prospect for work in the future, and say that he or she should not be asking why they are unemployed and how the Government will assist them, but should be asking how the Government will reduce the rate of inflation.
Since he is the one who is giving advice to the Government, it is little wonder it is stumbling, fumbling, and falling all over itself in terms of its fiscal and monetary policies. Obviously, the Government does not know what to do. It is afraid to venture out boldly and show that now is the time to invest in the productive capacity that will not only create jobs today but result in revenues coming to the senior levels of Government in the years ahead.
Let me give two examples. Every industrialized nation but two has launched an aggressive policy of railroad electrification. Those two exceptions are Canada and the United States. For all intents and purposes Canada is not interested in actively pursuing railroads electrification. Our hydro-electric potential in most regions of Canada is so extensive that there is export potential for generations into the future. It is a renewable and clean resource and one which Canada should be developing as part of its railroad system. Sweden has 99 per

I must give the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) credit since he has recently taken the initiative to provide some millions of dollars to assist the Province of British Columbia in electrifying the railway which moves coal from the northeast deposit sites down to the railroad systems.

As my colleague indicates, there will be some problems in terms of coal in the southwest, but the point is that I give the Government some credit for giving an indication that railroad electrification is a matter which should be considered. But what better time than now to launch a program of railroad electrification in this country? If such a program were started now, it would put people back to work in the manufacturing sector and on the railways. Since all the tunnels in western Canada will have to be increased in height, hundreds of thousands of steelworkers and miners will be put back to work for up to three years. That is the type of investment the Government should be considering now. That would not be wild Government spending but an investment in the future of the country. It will be done in the future but it will never be cheaper than it is today, and the employment is needed immediately.
Let me make another proposal, since Government Members opposite often accuse Members on this side of criticising the Government and not offering suggestions. I have just made one suggestion and I will make another one. Now is the time to launch a bold, imaginative and creative program in municipal public works across the country. Every municipality in the villages, towns, cities or metropolitan areas have plans on their books for new sewer systems, water systems, streets, sidewalks, parks, recreation centres, cultural centres, docks and marinas. Those plans exist and the implementation of those projects will put people to work immediately. They are not frivolous make-work projects since those projects will have to be undertaken eventually. They will not be any cheaper than they are now and the need for work will never be greater. They will result in returns to local, provincial and federal Governments in the future.
These projects represent investments in Canada's future. Members of Parliament, particularly from the NDP, have stated that the stimulation of our economy is the route the Government should follow. Let us see some serious and thoughtful stimulation not only in terms of short-term job creation but long-term job creation as well.
I want to say that we are not calling for the kind of make-work projects to which too often the Minister of Employment and Immigration relates and we are not talking about a project

simply to cut a trail for six months or to clean up a beach for six weeks. Those things can continue. We are talking about investment in Canada's future, investment in sound economic development proposals. One could go on and on with a litany of things. We have day after day laid out various proposals, but what do we hear from the Government and Members opposite? Are they concerned about the two million unemployed in this country? If they are, they ought to demonstrate what they are going to do about their plight. They ought to identify as a goal, in this budget that is coming in the next two weeks, full employment.
Canada is a country with 24 million people. It is the second largest land mass of any sovereign nation in the world and we have more resources per capita than any country in the world. If we cannot have a legitimate goal for employment, then no one can. Yet I do not hear Members opposite talking about a full employment option for Canada. Quite frankly, with all due respect to my Conservative colleagues, I do not hear them calling for a full employment option, a goal or an objective for this country. It is time to send a very clear signal to Canadians that full employment is our goal and outline the strategies to accomplish that goal.
However, we become rather disappointed when we hear time and time again that we cannot stimulate our economy, that we cannot take aggressive and bold measures to get Canadians working and to develop our economy in a serious way. We hear about restraint instead. It is interesting, Mr. Speaker, when you look at those folks advocating restraint and who say "Don't stimulate the economy; don't get Canadians back to work", that almost inevitably they are some of the most highly paid in Canada who are very secure in their jobs. One example is the head of Beil Canada, who said recently that Canadians are living with an unrealistic expectation syndrome. It sounds as though he has been coaching Governor Bouey of the Bank of Canada. Governor Bouey also spoke recently about Canadians having too high expectations.
However, two million Canadians simply want a job. Six hundred thousand young Canadians simply want to find a decent job for the first time in their life. Small businesses simply want to expand their operations. Farmers with small farms and ranches simply want to expand their operations or, as some of my colleagues say, they simply want to survive. Is this an unrealistic expectation? But notice that the man who says that Canadians should not be striving for these kinds of things makes only $600,000 a year as head of Bell Canada. Governor Bouey, the man who says "Hold off, bite the bullet, Canadians", tells two million people just to wait it out, that all is fine, and that they are asking the wrong questions anyway. He says to 600,000 young Canadians: "Just relax; eventually things will turn around". Granted, because he is protected by a salary in excess of $104,000 as he is hunkered down in that glass bunker of his protected from the real world, he can say those kinds of things.
It is a sad day when you hear people you should respect, people who ought to know better, suggesting to Canadians that these are the things they have to accept. I say that Canadians
do not have to accept these kinds of situations. Canada does not have to accept two million people out of work, a number that will increase as time goes on. Canada does not have to accept increasing personal bankruptcies, business bankruptcies and farm bankruptcies.
Back in 1972 the Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose), and more recently the Hon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway), pointed out what the Government of Canada was doing to the small farmer and small rancher. Because of the high interest rate policies of the Government of Canada, these people have been forced to leave their farms and seek employment elsewhere on a full or part-time basis. Perhaps a person has a small ranch in Central British Columbia, a family operation. The family consists of a husband, wife and two or three children. Perhaps they have 80, 90 or 100 head of cattle. They are trying to provide Canada with foodstuffs from one of the most critical sectors of the economy. They are trying to provide Canada with a vibrant, realistic and creative operation. Yet because of high interest rates, people like this have to leave the farm and find work in municipal work programs, in logging camps, on railroads, on highway crews, or wherever they can find work to subsidize the banks, to help meet those interest rate payments.
Then along comes Revenue Canada. These tax people who have sat in rabbit warrens in Ottawa for too long are now conducting audits across the country and saying to people: "This is not a full-time farming operation, it is part-time. You make more money off the farm than you do on the farm. Therefore, we have to tax you differently. You cannot have the tax deductions of a full-time ranch operation." Yet nothing has changed in terms of the operation. Just because these people are now seeking work outside, they cannot use the traditional deductions. The auditors tell people: "We are going to cut down your deductions." This will make it impossible for these people to be food producers and it will make it impossible for the family ranch to continue in operation. It will make it impossible for this most critical sector of the agriculture community to survive.
That is happening in western Canada today. I have received dozens and dozens of letters from people. My colleague the Hon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin has probably received more because of the number of ranchers in his constituency. The Hon. Member from Mission-Port Moody is experiencing the same thing. He has had letters from people saying they are being audited one, two, three and four years back.
What is the Government of Canada trying to do? The Government is trying to come before Parliament day after day to borrow more money. We are told that the Government is not going to indicate very clearly how the money will be spent. We hear Liberals say that they do not know what to do about the unemployment situation in this country; that they do not know how to build consumer and investor confidence. This Government wants to borrow $14 billion without even a statement as to how the money is to be raised and without even a statement as to where we are going in a budget.
This is a Government that decided to abandon all formal criteria in connection with coming to the House of Commons for borrowing authority. I remind the Government that it was only on May 31, 1982 that the former Minister of Finance said:
I would not expect the House to act upon an additional request for borrowing authority without providing it with detailed information on the economic situation and the implications of that situation on the government's fiscal situation. I do not think it would be appropriate to ask the House for additional borrowing authority until I have laid out in some detail an update of both the economic situation and the fiscal situation, and 1 certainly will be doing that before I would come back to the House for additional borrowing authority.
The information with respect to the situation for this current fiscal year of 1982-1983, the year ending on March 31 next, was finally pried out of Government at Committee. But the Government has not given us one iota of detail with respect to where we are going in 1983-1984. It is with that in mind that I thought I would address the House this morning, because we cannot in all justification, as elected Members of Parliament, properly vote for a Bill where all previous practise indicates that no such Bill should be produced. We cannot in all conscience, fulfilling our oath of requirement to our electors, allow the borrowing of money without accountability. We cannot allow the borrowing of money without a budget. When we do so we break with the whole tradition of parliamentary control over the financing of Government.
I think we should look at where we are going. We must look at the history. This Government has been in office for some 14 years now. Only one year in the past 14 has it managed not to show a deficit. In good years it borrowed and borrowed and borrowed, and when we have a recession in some countries and a depression in this country, it borrows more and more and more.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what we have to do today and through the next month is determine where we are going as a country. What we have to do is determine what obligations there are for a Government to perform. I think we would all agree that it is necessary for Government to defend its people from foreigners, to protect its soil, to protect the integrity of its country, to make sure that law and order are in place. We do not do a very good job of that. I think we would all agree that it is necessary for Government in this world, certainly today, to look after the sick and the weak in our society, to make sure that those who are incapable of really looking after their own affairs in terms of their financial health are able to get by, to have a reasonable standard of living, to be reasonably well cared for, to be reasonably well housed. I think we will agree that it is important that we educate our children so that they will be able to carry on in our place, build our country, make

March 29, 1983
Borrowing Authority
our country a progressive place and contribute to world society.
Beyond that, I think it is about time we started looking to what other things Government should be doing and to what extent is Government essential beyond that. Is it Government's function to interfere in the means of distribution and the manufacture of products? Is it Government's duty to be involved in the business community? Is it Government's obligation to make grants to transport companies owned by its friends? Is it Government's duty to look after those who could look after themselves but would rather have the taxpayer bail them out? Is it not time that we as a nation, that we as a Parliament, put some priorities on where we spend Government funds and how we allow money that is borrowed at exceedingly high rates, borrowed on the credit of our children and our children's children, to be spent? Is it not fair that we examine where our priorities are, where we should be going and what Government should be doing? What are the limits of Government?
Can we really expect to carry on when the proportion that we as a society allocate to the management of its affairs by Government has now crept up to very close to 50 per cent of the Gross National Product? Can we really justify situations where federally-owned Crown corporations alone control $34 billion worth of business in a year? That is not taking into account provincial Crown corporations such as hydro corporations and the like.
I think it is about time that we as a nation started looking at what our needs are. What are our needs? Some people say they need a holiday. My wife says we need a new dryer. My daughter thinks she needs a new car. Where are needs? We look around at what this Government spends; we go to certain Ministers' offices. I see the Minister of Transport is here; I had an opportunity when we were the Government to go to the top of his high flying office space. Tie has an office where you could bury your feet in the carpets.

speechtext:
Somewhere along the line we must priorize where we are going. What are we doing with this money that the Government wants to borrow? What has happened is that we have gone wrong in the way we manage of our country. We have gone to a situation where somehow Government determines that the needs of Departments are all of a sudden absolute needs that must be financed by taxes and borrowing. If you cannot tax enough you borrow, and it does not really matter because it is a need that must be financed. Therefore it must be borrowed. I suggest that the way we have been
operating this country is to get each Department to produce an estimate, wrap those estimates in blue paper and call them the Blue Book, and say that they are the estimates of Government expenditure, they are our needs and they must somehow be financed, no matter what. That is no longer possible, if it ever was possible; but today it has gone beyond reason.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) says that our GNP last year was an estimated $348 billion. There is really no indication of any huge increase in GNP for the 1983 year. Some indicators show we may have growth of 1 per cent, some 0.5 per cent. No one is saying that the economy will break forth and grow by any consequential amount.
What happens to Government estimates of spending? On a budgetary basis, the Blue Book estimates filed by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) indicates that we will spend close to $90 billion. We all know that budgetary expenditures are part of the tale. We should be looking at the national accounts expenditures, but we are not given those figures. If we compare national accounts with budgetary accounts in the past year, we note that budgetary accounts understate real expenditures by between 10 and 15 per cent. If budgetary accounts are in the neighbourhood of $90 billion, the real expenditure of Government will be in excess of $105 billion. One does not have to be very bright, grade six or seven, I suppose, to tell that if the Government is going to spend $105 billion and we only have a GNP of $348 billion, Government expenditures will likely be in excess of 30 per cent of the GNP.
What about the Provinces and municipalities? Where are we headed? The Government wraps its needs in blue paper, calls it a Blue Book, says it has done some estimates and budgetary control. The fact is that it has not. When anyone wants their office reupholstered, it is done. When the Government wants a new Challenger jet, it gets one. When Canadair is going South, it gets more money. When a Liberal friend who owns a trucking company gets in trouble, they bail him out. That is the kind of "control" this House can no longer tolerate.
Some say we have developed the British disease. The Brits have all of a sudden awakened. At one point in Great Britain the percentage of GNP devoted to deficit was very close to 10 per cent. Sir Geoffrey Howe's latest budget indicates that the British deficit will now be less than 2.5 per cent of the gross domestic product.
Where is ours going? Last year it was 7.8 per cent. What will it be next year? We do not know, yet we are being asked to finance it. If the trend line continues, it will be 10 or 11 per cent. The British have moved up their status in terms of credit worthiness. They have replaced us and are now fifth. The British have reduced their rate of inflation from 18 or 19 per cent to less than 5 per cent. What have we done? We have six and five, you know! But six and five does not apply to Government expenditures. That would not be possible. At a minimum, it is 9.8 per cent on a budgetary basis. If you look at it year
March 29, 1983

over year, it is 17.8 per cent. We have six and five, but I think it is six time five in two years. That is the way the Government has increased its expenditures. It does not care and does not get down to things.
Some say we should borrow money to stimulate the economy. Let us look at what stimulation this borrowing has done. In 1968 when the Prime Minister took over, 358,000 Canadians were unemployed. In February, nearly 1.6 million Canadians were unemployed. All we did was borrow more, stimulate more and encourage more; more enterprise development programs, more hand-outs, more grant and loan programs, stimulating housing this way or that. The Government has tried to stimulate by its borrowing.
Do you know what happens when you borrow? When the Government borrows, it raises interest rates for ordinary commercial people because it bids up interest rates. What does the Government do when it bids it up? It squanders it. It does not create any new products, businesses or industries. It does not create anything new. What productivity, product or new creation can the Government show? The British can say that they have a productive Government, one that has reduced the civil service by 65,000 since 1979. This Government boasts of the fact that it has only increased its employment by 1 per cent this year.
This Government has no control over its appetite, its waste or spending. It has no priorizing of any activity it undertakes. Time and again we have asked the Government to form a special committee of this House of Commons with responsible parliamentarians, similar to the committee of the United States Congress which goes over proposed budgets, the proposed totality of spending, so as to priorize those expenditures, cross-examine officials about them, reduce them. In that way we could get our spending down to what we can afford. This Government has refused for the very simple reason that it does not believe in control. It has some idea that all will be well because it can still continue to borrow.
I see, Mr. Speaker, you are signalling that my time is up. Let me conclude by saying that the Bill before us cannot and should not be passed. A responsible Government would not even present it. Responsible Members of Parliament, regardless of Party affiliation, should vote against it. I call upon this House this afternoon to defeat this Bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I spoke on Bill C-143 on earlier occasions, I indicated that there are two aspects that Canadians find most disturbing. First, they believe that the financial management of this country is out of control. As a result, they firmly believe that as taxpayers they are not getting a fair deal. They are not getting fair value for the money that is spent for them by the Government of Canada. That view is shared not only by an increasing number of Canadians, but it is shared by the current Auditor General and the late former Auditor General.
Those of us in the House share that view because Parliament has lost effective control of the public purse. This is the 21st or
Borrowing Authority
22nd time that closure has been invoked in this House this session, and on most of those occasions it was invoked on a measure having to do with taxation, amendments to the Income Tax Act or the principle of extracting revenue from the Canadian public.
Crown corporations, which the Auditor General described as a form of sub-government, are not accountable to their shareholders, namely the public of Canada. Even though we have modified the Committee structure and reformed parliamentary rules, there does not seem to be adequate provisions to ensure that Crown corporations are made accountable to Parliament and, thereby, to the people of Canada. The result is that there is a perception that the Government goes on its very merry way recklessly spending the hard-earned tax dollars which it collects from Canadian taxpayers. It does this without satisfying those taxpayers that the money it is spending on their behalf is being spent with some consideration and regard to economy and efficiency. Look at its acquisition of a string of service stations! I recall that the former Minister of Energy said in introducing the Bill on Petro-Canada that it would not be Government's intention to get involved in the retail gas business. That, to me, meant we would not be in the retail service station business. Today we probably have more than 3,000 bought and paid for by the taxpayers of Canada. Government has a very glamorous and expensive advertising budget. I am not suggesting that it is not important for the Government to advertise, but I believe there is a prevailing view among the taxpayers of Canada that it can be cut significantly.
There is concern about the double standard which is applied to industry with respect to bail-outs, there is one rule for the Maislins, the Massey-Fergusons and the Domes of the world, but there is another rule applied to the small family farm, the small family business and the other enterprises which have heretofore been productive in generating wealth and jobs.
What all this means, Mr. Speaker, in total, is that the excessive amount of Government spending on a national accounts basis has risen by 67 per cent since this Liberal Government was returned to office in February, 1980. That is why we are being asked to approve the borrowing of some $19 billion in this Bill. That is why today that for every three dollars we spend, one dollar of that expenditure is borrowed money; or 34 per cent of our expenditures by the Government of Canada is borrowed money. That is why as well, Mr. Speaker, that for every five dollars that the Government spends, one dollar goes to pay the interest on the debt. That national debt, on a gross basis, has now risen to somewhere in the vicinity of $160 billion to $165 billion. That compares with a figure of $31 billion when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) assumed office.
I would like to speak about the deficits which have been chalked up since this Government was returned to office. For the fiscal year 1980-81 there was a deficit of $12.6 billion. In the fiscal year 1981-82 there was a deficit of $13.6 billion. In fiscal year 1982-83 there was a deficit of $27.2 billion. In this

March 29, 1983
Borrowing Authority
current fiscal year there is a projected deficit of $30 billion. In total that amounts to some $83.5 billion.
My colleague the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) referred to the fact that one of the ways of comparing our performance, or our record of financial control, is by comparing ourselves to other industrialized nations, and one way of measuring the depth of our deficit is by measuring it against our gross domestic product. As my colleague pointed out, in 1981 our deficit was equal to something in the order of 3 per cent of the gross domestic product. As a matter of fact, it was 2.8 per cent. In 1982-83 that figure has risen to 8 per cent of the gross domestic product. When I say gross domestic product, I mean all the goods and services which are produced within the boundaries of Canada. So we are at 8 per cent now and with the projection of a $30 billion deficit it could rise to something in the order of 10 per cent. Ten per cent of our gross domestic product will comprise our deficit in this fiscal year.
The United States is seriously worried about its deficit and is making some very heavy expenditures on defence and a whole host of programs for economic recovery. The United States has projected its deficit to equal something in the order of 5 per cent to 6 per cent of its total gross domestic product. Britain, which has had its share of financial difficulties, just recently halved its deficit from 5.5 per cent in 1978-79 to 2.75 per cent of its gross domestic product. Therefore, that indicates, Mr. Speaker, that Canada is following a trend line which is out of step with its industrialized neighbours.
With this kind of a record it is no wonder that we in this country have the second highest rate of unemployment in the industrialized world. It is no wonder that we have the third highest rate of inflation in the industrialized world. It is no wonder that we have higher interest rates than most other industrialized nations of the world, and the highest misery rate of any industrialized nation in the world. We have the lowest generation of growth on a per capita basis. It is now something equal to less than the share which we achieved in 1976.
Another aspect, of course, Mr. Speaker, which disturbs Canadians is the fact that they do not believe that the impact of the recession we are currently expriencing is being shared fairly by all components of society. To Canadians there is little evidence that Government, its bureaucracies, its enterprises, its activities in those areas which are under the control or under the thumb of Government, are feeling the pain of recession which those people in the private sector are. We can take as an example wages and salaries. Notwithstanding the six and five program, we know that 40 per cent of those employed by Government received increases of well in excess of six and five and closer to 10 per cent. Statistics Canada recently reported that public sector wages rose by 15.9 per cent this year over last year versus a figure of 5.8 per cent in the private sector. Another recent study indicated that in the area of small business, one-third of small business managers had no increase in salary last year; one-third had a decrease; the others maintained the status quo. As far as their employees were concerned, two-thirds of them in small business had reductions in
salary or their increases postponed. One in five had increases of less than 6 per cent.
When we consider the burden of unemployment and the pain associated with it, as my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South indicated, in the area of Government employment rose by 1 per cent. But we all know what has happened out there in the real world. Here again, there has been very little impact upon Government enterprises.
Recently the Canadian Federation of Independent Business pointed out that 50 per cent of the unemployed, somewhere in the vicinity of 700,000 to 800,000 people, have been laid off from the small business sector. Of course, I am sure there are many owner-managers who were laid off as a result of their business going down the tube, forced into bankruptcy and liquidation.
Speaking of bankruptcies, well in excess of 10,000 businesses, 91 per cent more than in 1979, were chalked up on the bankruptcy rolls last year in Canada. Over 400 farmers went bankrupt, and that does not tell the whole story because there are many who have gone out of business voluntarily. Look at the prices controlled by Government regulation, Mr. Speaker. They are not subject to the vagaries of the marketplace, so as a result they have increased by something in the order of 16 per cent to 17 per cent while the price component in the real marketplace increased by something in the order of 8 per cent.
What I am saying, Mr. Speaker, is that the burden of the recession is being shared in a very lopsided fashion. The producers, the innovators, the generators of wealth in this country, are suffering while the spenders are being rewarded.
I say to you, sir, that if there was clear evidence coming from the Government that it was seriously attacking waste, extravagance and inefficiency, if it was serious about equalizing this burden, I think there could be some sympathy for this Bill. If there was a clear indication that this Government was moving to reduce the over-all burden of Government in Canada and its cost to the individual taxpayer, there might be some justification for this particular measure. If there was included in these programs, for which the Government wants this money, something to improve the fortunes of the small-business sector, the farmer, the innovator, the entrepreneur, the job creator, I think we could look at this bill in a more positive light.
The small business sector is hurting, Mr. Speaker. So is the agricultural sector, which up to this point is the only industry which could be a bright spot in Canada. When you look at the importance of agriculture, it is absolutely shameful that we make such a trivial effort to support and enhance the industry. While agriculture employs only 5 per cent of the population directly, the agri-food business accounts for 18 per cent of the total labour force in this country and 40 per cent of the total economic activity. The spin-off benefits are enormous. Yet we see the Government bringing in a measure to increase the freight rate for the movement of grain. We see a Government
March 29, 1983

which has imposed a very heavy burden by way of energy taxes. I see my hon. friend across the way who has been championing the plight of those who are less fortunate. I refer specifically to his initiative with respect to Bill C-653, and I congratulate him for his efforts. Some may disagree with the content of the Bill, but no one can question the sincerity of the Hon. Member. He is clearly trying to do something to help the Canadian farmer, but it is kind of a last resort.

speechtext:
A first step. Well, the Member knows we share his view and we certainly are supporting his efforts in that regard. But we need something more to assist our young farmers and those who are facing financial difficulties, those who have been locked into high interest rates. There has to be a mechanism to assist them in extricating themselves from that unfortunate occurrence. There must be some federal Government initiative to provide some help in that regard.
We have also called for the establishment of an agri-bond program which would provide medium-term credit at a lower rate of interest. Time and time again we have called for a massive reduction if not a total elimination of taxes on farm fuels used in the production of food. When I talk about farm fuels, I am not merely talking about diesel fuel and gasoline; I am talking about natural gas which is used in the manufacture of fertilizer and in the operation of greenhouses. It is a crippling burden on the producers of Canada. The Government could provide relief in that area.
We are calling as well for the Government to maintain, in view of current difficulties, the current level of initial grain prices in this country so farmers can plan with some degree of confidence. We have also asked time and again for legislation-we agreed that we would pass a Bill with one day's debate-to double the farm cash advances for grain sold through the Canadian Wheat Board. That would provide some measure of confidence for the future. We have also maintained that the Government should move ahead with its beef stabilization program in conjunction with the Provinces. We believe that is something that could be done to provide some stability and confidence in that very important sector.
So there is much that could be done, Mr. Speaker. There is much that needs to be done. If some of these measures were incorporated into the Government's program, I think we could look at this Bill in a different light. But since the Government is wanting to borrow on the basis of a blank cheque, without telling us what it is going to do and how it is going to do it, and simply continue its wasteful, extravagant and irresponsible expenditures, there is no way that we can support this measure. Therefore, it is for that reason that I have risen today to speak out against this Bill and to speak out against this Government. It has completely lost touch with the reality out there.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I see they are starting to warm up a little on the other side. It seems
Borrowing Authority
to happen every time I rise in the House. My Progressive Conservative friends get all excited, and of course I do occasionally say things that upset them a little bit. I would not want to hurt the sensitive ears of these poor little Progressive Conservatives who are either against the metric system or for bilingualism but do not want to spend any money on it-they are a mass of inconsistencies. I have asked your permission, Mr. Speaker, to speak again this week because as a good Member of Parliament who represents his riding and who comes to the House to listen to the debate, I have a few comments to make on what is being said about the Government's borrowing authority request.
Mr. Speaker, up to now we have spent exactly fourteen days on this debate. The House has been sitting fourteen days to consider the Government's request for a borrowing authority of $19 billion. The previous speaker gave a typical example of the incoherence that is rife in the Progressive Conservative Party. But first of all, we had the Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) who told us that we had to fire 65,000 public servants, cut Government spending and stop everything. The next Member who spoke told the House that new policies had to be designed to spend even more money, to help farmers borrow money and to help beef and grain producers. The same incoherence is apparent every year. I just wonder because obviously, if the Government is asking for authority to borrow $19 billion, it is because it has made an undertaking, through its policies, to distribute money to Canadians, and we have been saying this all along. Every year, another debate forces the Government to impose closure, and every year we hear the same old speeches. This year, I heard some Hon. Members repeating the speeches they made the week before on the same subject, with basically the same rhetoric and a few variations here and there. It is incredible that the House of Commons should have to spend fourteen days on this question. As far as 1 am concerned, I would like to hear one Member of the Official Opposition and one Member of the New Democratic Party express clearly and simply the respective positions of their parties for the Canadian public. The Government would then give its position, a vote would be held and that would be the end of it, because in any case, the Members of the Opposition know perfectly well that the Canadian Government must act on the legislation passed by Parliament, no matter whether Parliament was right or wrong in passing the legislation. If legislation is passed requiring the Canadian Government to pay for medical services, the Government must do so.
Every year, they take advantage of the fact that the Government is obliged to ask Parliament for borrowing authority because there are deficits, and hold long drawn out debates for fourteen days, Mr. Speaker. Imagine! I am not going to dwell any longer on the subject, but it has been taking as long as the bells crisis. All this to vote on whether or not the Government will be given the requested borrowing authority, and when Opposition Members tell us that they were willing to have a

March 29, 1983
Borrowing Authority
quick debate, provided the Government spends more money on agriculture, provided it spends more here and more there- finally, it all ends with the Opposition saying that it does not make sense to let the Government borrow $19 billion, that is just too much money, it does not make sense and it is just giving them a blank cheque. The incoherence of it all is really incredible. It is like a yard full of turkeys who are running back and forth, trying to establish some kind of totally incongruous pecking order. From time to time, we do hear the occasional good speech, which helps to restore a modicum of logic to the debate. However, looking back on what has been achieved during the past four years-my first years in the House-and considering the number of days spent on discussing the issue of the Government's borrowing authority, I wish I could count the number of times a Member of the Official Opposition has said: I refuse to give the Federal Government a blank cheque.
Every time a Member opposite says those words, and they are repeated several times in the course of a single speech- they have been using the same words for four years, and it makes no sense at all, because as Members of Parliament they ought to know how our money is spent. They are supposed to know, unless they are not doing their job, because as Members of this House, we are close to the Canadian people and we are in the best position to know where every cent spent by the Government is going. If my hon. friends in the Official Opposition do not know where that money is going, either they are not doing their job in committee or they never go home to their job in their ridings. Mr. Speaker, it is always the same Members who are asking for more money. Just look at question period. At least half, if not all, of the questions are put by Members asking the Federal Government to spend more money or asking the Government why it did not spend more. The Members of the New Democratic Party are incredible in this respect. All they do is ask for money!
I was listening just now to one of their Members who was asking the Government to electrify all the railways in Canada. Not a bad idea, but, Mr. Speaker, I am taking the position of a Quebecer who has seen Mr. Parizeau making Quebec residents who are further away from the Ontario border pay more than $1 taxes on a gallon of gas, which is blackmail, because they have to go to the gas station. If tomorrow morning, all the railways in Quebec were to be electrified, it would mean that once again, the people of that Province would be liable to be blackmailed by Mr. Parizeau, because electric power is a provincial monopoly across Canada. The Provinces set the prices through their provincial transport commissions, and that is the kind of situation the Hon. Member wants to get us into. I am inclined to be a bit reticent. People have been talking about the Canadian Government's deficit and comparing our country to countries like Great Britain-which is hard-pressed to operate normally three days a week-and we are being compared to our neighbours to the south and to other countries with the same economic system, and people seem to be saying
that Canada's performance has been very poor. But there are major differences which they forget to point out to the Canadian people. There is not a single country where the national Government gives a blank cheque to the provinces. Does anyone know that our Progressive Conservative friends never speak about their colleagues who are provincial Premiers? We never hear anything about them, and yet several of them now hold office. Several of those people are provincial Premiers, genuine Tories, including a few who even want to lead the national Party and who are now heading provincial Governments. They never tell the Canadian people that the provinces unilaterally decide what they will spend for health insurance or post-secondary, college and university education without even consulting Ottawa about it, and all we get here at the end are the bills. They forget to mention that all those cash transfers represent this year an expenditure of almost $ 18 billion for the Canadian Government. They forget to say that Canada is the only country which has shown enough respect for its provincial institutions to give them the power to spend and to implement provincial policies which, by their own admission, are tailored to their own personality and their own requirements. They forget to point out that the Federal Government accounts for nearly 80 per cent of the budget of a province such as Newfoundland. They forget to say that, Mr. Speaker. Why? Because those provinces are led by their own friends.
Let us try the American system since that is what the Progressive Conservative Members want. Let municipalities pay for schools as they do in the United States. Let spokesmen for a city similar to New York tell us: We are going to be near bankruptcy tomorrow, help us. That is the experiment those people want to try. What makes our country so great, Mr. Speaker, is indeed the fact that a Canadian owns a part of Canada, no matter where he lives. His origin, his religion, his culture, his tongue and his colour do not matter at all, as long as he is a resident of a great country called Canada where resources are plentiful. All that makes up a national Government which has the responsibility to support each and every Canadian as well as our Canadian institutions, be they provincial, municipal or otherwise.
As a resident of Quebec, I have a problem on my hands- perhaps my colleagues from the other provinces are in a similar predicament, but I am not sure-in that municipalities in Quebec no longer have the right to speak to the Canadian Government, because they are told that they fall under Quebec City's jurisdiction. We have just had another experience, this time related to the NEED Program under which the Canadian Government will spend $170 million in the province. We have tried to co-operate with the provincial authorities and explain to them that they would contribute $45 million and administer the whole program jointly with us in such fields as non-profit corporations. Normally, we would not need you, we could choose to act unilaterally, but we will administer the program
March 29, 1983

in co-operation with you and live a common experience. The outcome of the common experience is that after three months of delays we are forced to answer: Very well, give your $45 million to the municipalities by yourselves and we shall invest our $170 million in non-profit-making corporations, private companies and Federal Departments. Why? Because we, in Quebec, also have people with closed minds.
The Progressive Conservatives are not the only people who oppose the metric system and have a closed mind. We also have such people. There are people in Quebec who say: The municipalities belong to Quebec. If a mayor is elected, he must deal with his MLA. He must not speak to the Federal Member of Parliament because he must not deal directly with the Government of Canada. He has no right to do so. This is the type of constraint which we have to deal with in Quebec, with the result that useful policies which normally could be applied in a spirit of co-operation in a well-structured manner by both levels of governments have to be applied unilaterally, that is by us on one side and them on the other. We have about the same experience. I would like to quote a comment by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) when he was wondering what would become of co-operative federalism which the Liberals under Mr. Pearson had so well promoted by giving the provinces certain taxation powers as well as health insurance and post-secondary education programs for which the Canadian Government guaranteed to pay at least 50 per cent of the cost. Where are we going and why? The provinces have administered these programs in such a way that their purpose is now completely distorted. Look at Quebec! Our hospitals are now completely run down. I shall not tell you what is going on in my own constituency, but it is almost catastrophic. Look at what is happening in education. Recently, all Quebec public servants have been blamed by the Quebec Government. Apparently, they are guilty, but of what? They are guilty of having accepted the wages imposed by their own provincial Government. Now they are guilty. They are being blamed by this same Government. Why? God knows! Why was all this accepted? What is wrong today was good yesterday. Mr. Parizeau himself said so when the last collective agreement was signed: "We signed for peanuts." He is now telling these people: "You are robbing the state; I shall take away 20 per cent of your wages."
Such things are clearly unacceptable and this raises a few questions for the central Government. I want to ask my hon. friends opposite, who have friends among the leaders of provincial parties, and friends who are heading some of our provincial governments, to ask their own parties to think about the kind of administrative powers the Federal Government has given them during the last 20 years and where those powers are taking them. What route do they want to take? Are they trying to prove that a country like Canada should not give more powers to the Provinces or are they perhaps trying to prove the opposite?
Borrowing Authority
Personally, I am all for having the Provinces develop their own powers and preserving their charateristics, but when I see what is happening in Quebec, where the tax burden has become absolutely incredible, and the billions of dollars that are being taken from the Caisse de depot du Quebec to buy companies, to bring in companies like Pechiney in Becancour, to take over companies like Alcan in my area and to compete in Quebec with our own companies that are already being forced to lay off workers, I really cannot begin to express my feelings about this. I will never be able to agree with policies that are based solely on Government power, not on the welfare of the people. Coherent policies are absolutely necessary, if we are to run this country the way it should be run. The Provinces will have to discharge their responsibilities, Mr. Speaker, and the Opposition parties will have to stop their little cat-and-mouse game. They will have to stop telling the Federal Government it is spending too much, when the vast majority of federal expenditures goes directly to the Provinces, who are their own political friends, and who are spending the money. There will have to be more consistency, because the party opposite has spent the last four years between two leaders. They will have to choose a leader who will determine their party's political destiny. The Members opposite will have to stop telling us that the price of oil is too low in Canada, as they were saying three years ago, and now the price has gone up, we are killing the oil industry because we have set prices too high.
They will have to clarify their stand on a number of issues. If they want the oil industry to function properly, they will have to ask the Canadian Government to abolish the Provinces' authority to levy taxes on gas, because their own political friends who are heading their own Provincial Governments, as in Ontario, for instance, are levying gas taxes and adding to the taxpayers' burden, while they are also killing the oil industry. They know all this, but our friends opposite are not raising these issues in the House.
Mr. Speaker, I am certainly not afraid to ask my Government to restrain provincial powers with respect to gas taxes. It is really incredible! And when I see the New Democratic Party come up with one of its pipe dreams that we should electrify the railways, when I know perfectly well that when Mr. Parizeau decides to sell power to the Canadian Government to run the trains, those kilowatts are going to be so expensive that not a single train will be running in Quebec, I fail to see any consistency in that. It is unbelievable! As if that were not enough, year in and year out we are forced to waste 10 or 15 days of debate on a borrowing Bill which is required to help needy Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I said last week and I say again today that I am proud to be a Liberal because the policies which we are now implementing and which cost a bundle to the Canadian Government are designed to help the population. I would be ashamed of myself if I had to return to my riding tomorrow

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, within the next few months, Cabinet will decide on the final adjudication of a contract for the construction of six frigates for the Department of National Defence.
On behalf of the people of the Quebec City area and the riding of Levis, I would like to point out to the Government that this $3 billion contract will have economic spinoffs that are of considerable interest to Quebecers who expect, and rightly so, to benefit quite substantially from the contract. speechtext:

More specifically, on behalf of the Federation des producteurs maraichers, the Syndicat des producteurs de fraises et de framboises du Quebec, the Federation des producteurs de pommes du Quebec, the Federation des producteurs de pommes de terre du Quebec, the Syndicat des producteurs en serres du Quebec, the Federation des producteurs de bleuets du Quebec, and also on behalf of the Federation des producteurs de fruits et de legumes du Quebec,
I want to ask the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) to act on a request sent by telegram, asking the Minister to reinstate Section 16 of the Unemployment Insurance Regulations, since the absence of this section seems to be seriously hurting both farmers and farm workers. In the circumstances, and in view of other representations made by Members of this House, I hope the Minister will realize the importance of this issue and will agree to this request, for the benefit of these workers and producers.

Madam Speaker, as reported in today's press, the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Ontario suggested that couples should take publicly sponsored premarital courses in an attempt to cut the social and economic cost of divorces. This suggestion, in my view, is something that should be supported by Parliamentarians. The suggestion no doubt emanates from the appalling statistics on the ever-increasing divorce rate in Canada. Recently, as reported by Statistics Canada, 40 per cent of Canadian marriages end up in divorce. These rates have been eroding away at the family as the foundation of our social framework and should be cause for grave concern on the part of this House.
Given this statement and the statistics, I would urge the Government, through the Department of Justice, to take very seriously the recommendation and any others that might be made that would have the effect of bolstering the family as a strong and stable social unit and, through that means, the Canadian social fabric.
In addition to facilitating the dissolution of marriages which are inretrievably damaged, the Government should be leaving no stone unturned to ensure that the strength of the basic building block of our society is supported and encouraged.

Madam Speaker, Canada's prison staff must, day in and day out, maintain a patient and understanding relationship with a shifting and sometimes dangerous population, and must take the brunt of unacceptable conditions such as double bunking and severe overcrowding, as well as suffer frustrations, aggravations, and anxieties beyond most occupations. In a recent meeting with some 90 officers and guards, I was told that 50 per cent of
