these worries are caused, created, and aggravated by regional and headquarters staff, many of whom have no idea of what actually goes on inside prison walls.
For example, the staff in the Drumheller Institution have, over the years, worked out an excellent duty roster, with which the staff and the administration are happy. Just recently the Commissioner of Penitentiaries decreed that all institutions must operate on a seven day on and three day off, seven day on and four day off rotation. This system, instead of reducing the abuse and solving problems, is creating aggravation and dissatisfaction among the staff.
The squad system used by the Drumheller Institution has many advantages over the proposed system which I cannot enumerate now because of the time restriction. Suffice it to say that it has worked well and is working well, and there is no need for blanket uniform procedures when this one is doing the job.
I urge the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) to overrule the Commissioner and permit the continued use of the squad system, which will help greatly in dealing with the severe problems this staff is already facing due to overcrowding, and a mixture of medium offenders with dangerous criminals.

Madam Speaker, at the meeting of the Senate and Commons Standing Committees on External Affairs and National Defence with the Prime Minister of Greece, a number of concerns of this House were discussed which are of particular concern to many of my constituents who are of Greek origin.
Prime Minister Papandreou raised several problems of security in the eastern Mediterannean, First, Cyprus, where 34.6 per cent of the territory is still occupied by Turkish troops despite United Nations resolutions and bilateral talks. Canada's ongoing role as peacekeeper is crucial until a secure peace is achieved.
Canadians who want Canada to be recognized as a nuclear-free zone will be encouraged by Greece's efforts in the same direction and, indeed, for a broad Balkan-wide nuclear-free zone, which would desirably join up with a nuclear-free zone in northern Europe.
More negatively, there was also discussion of the possibility of a serious imbalance of forces in the Aegean, with increased American military aid to Turkey. And, although Mr. Papandreou did not say it, it is well known that the threat of increased military strength in Turkey is a means of pressuring Greece to keep its American bases, a decision that Greeks should be able to make on their own for their own reasons.
My Party welcomes the Prime Minister's visit, both as an opportunity to discuss important international questions, and
Greek-Canada relations, and to see an old friend again. We are delighted also that Mrs. Margaret Papandreou, who is the President of the Women's Union of Greece is part of the visit.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: IMPROVEMENTS NEEDED AT HAMILTON CIVIC AIRPORT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, regional airports play a vital role in Canada's air transportation system, yet the performance of this important function is diminished considerably in some such airports for want of updated facilities. At the Hamilton Civic Airport, for example, inadequate runway and approach lighting often forces Nor-dair, the airport's only major airline, to cancel flights in and out of Hamilton and to divert flights to Toronto in bad weather, at a high cost to the airline and inconvenience to Nordair passengers. Given high intensity approach lights and sequential flashing strobes, I believe that many cancellations could be avoided, and possibly other airlines would look at Hamilton Civic Airport more favourably.
Since this type of infrastructural development is vital to the growth of the Hamilton community, I strongly urge the Department of Transport to investigate this situation and to install additional approach and runway lighting at the Airport as soon as possible.

Madam Speaker, about 18 months ago the Canadian Shipbuilding & Ship Repairing Association conducted a domestic shipbuilding survey covering market requirements through the 1980s. The survey showed a requirement for over 400 new ships and floating equipment at a cost in 1981 dollars of $33 billion plus.
Of this amount, the Government's projected requirements accounted for $3 billion. On the surface this augured well for our future. However, instead of full order books and healthy employment levels, we see some 6,000 fewer men and women at work in our Canadian shipyards today than one year ago. Why? One reason can be found in the 80 per cent grants policy for exploration of gas and oil and its supporting equipment. We see PetroCan selling its offshore service boats, for example, in order to lease back and gain the advantage of the 80 per cent grant which is not available through private acquisition and ownership. Esso, as well, has seen the advantage of this, and is operating through Citibank. Husky Oil, as well, has equipment up for sale. It wants to sell it offshore and lease it back. What does this do? Who loses? I will tell you who loses. There are no orders in the Halifax shipyards.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bob Kaplan (Solicitor General of Canada):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF OFFENDERS BEFORE RELEASE FROM PRISON
speechtext: Madam Speaker, what the Hon. Member is asking for is something that I think is impossible in a democratic society, that is, that a person who has been given a punishment by a court and served that punishment should, at the order of an executive, without committing any additional offence, have his incarceration continued. subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Bill C-143, which we are now debating, seeks to give the federal Government authority to borrow $19 billion. This legislation represents the largest borrowing Bill in the history of Canada. Never before has the Government been required to come to Parliament, cap in hand, for the authority to borrow such a massive amount of money. The reason it must do this is that never before has the Government been so broke or the Canadian economy so badly mismanaged.
In the time I have available I want to focus on the area of Government waste and extravagance to which I made reference a few moments ago during Oral Question Period. That area concerns the operations of Transport Canada, and Canadian National in particular. I want to focus on this area of spending and waste because it, more so than any other that I can think of, threatens what little fiscal responsibility remains in the Government of Canada. I am referring more generally to that labyrinth of sub-government commonly known as Crown corporations.
The current Government has allowed Crown corporations to become so plentiful and so large and so unaccountable that it was utterly incapable of providing the Opposition with even a ballpark estimate of the number of such agencies that actually exist at the federal level. Nowhere is the problem more acute than in my own backyard, the Atlantic Provinces, vis-a-vis CN Marine.
CN Marine is an independent profit centre of its parent company, Canadian National. In the Atlantic Provinces its primary function is to operate ferry services from one Province to another. In my Province of Prince Edward Island, CN Marine operates a car ferry service across the 14-mile Northumberland Strait, which separates the Island from New Brunswick.
The most famous of the Corporation's several ferries is the icebreaker Abegweit. When it was built in 1947, it was the world's largest and most powerful icebreaker of its kind. Since then she has earned a special place in the hearts and minds of Islanders, for she has served us well. On the worst days of our sometimes brutal winters, the tenacious "Abby", as she is affectionately called, has kept us from being totally cut off from the rest of Canada.
I mention the Abegweit because now, after 35 years since her maiden crossing, the Abegweit is being replaced by the Abegweit //, a spanking new vessel out of the Saint John Shipbuilding and Drydock. As the Auditor General made only

March 29, 1983
Borrowing Authority
too clear in his celebrated 1982 Report, the new Abegweit has come to symbolize Government ineptitude, waste and extravagance every bit as much as the old Abby symbolized dependability and service.
The facts are as follows. The Department of Transport paid some S25 million, as a partial payment toward the total cost of the vessel, to CN Marine ostensibly as an upfront advance payment to the builder for the stated purpose of achieving savings of $2.9 million in anticipated cost escalations. However, instead of advancing the $25 million to the shipbuilder immediately, as CN Marine was committed to do, the corporation stashed the funds in a special interest-bearing bank account for a time. The interest earned on the money deposited accumulated to an amount in excess of $4.8 million. That most of the money was eventually applied to the capital cost of the vessel does not mitigate one iota the fact that CN Marine's actions were utterly irresponsible and self-serving.
In effect, CN Marine used public funds to amass hundreds of thousands of dollars to which it was not entitled through a sleight-of-hand that flew in the face of every accepted Government accounting practice, even by the lax standards of this incompetent Government. To boot, CN Marine paid the shipbuilder $163,000 to consent to the arrangement. Some may call that an inducement or moral suasion, but I call it an outright bribe.
As if the situation were not bad enough, which it clearly is, CN Marine and CN have stonewalled all efforts by the Government's Auditor General to obtain information about the funding of the Abegweit. The Auditor General has determined that CN Marine's handling of the cash advance from the Department of Transport, though done ostensibly in the name of frugality and of saving the Government money, realized not one cent of savings on the total cost of the vessel in question.
Moreover, the Auditor General has seriously questioned the ethics of an agency of the Crown paying $163,000 to a shipbuilder from a special trust account that it was not entitled to set up in the first place.
The point is that, while the Abegweit incident may have little effect in the context of the Government's $90 billion budget, such practices could cause the Government significant problems if all of the hundreds of other Crown corporations conducted their affairs in the same manner. And many of them do so. A former senior Government auditor, now retired, whom I trust implicitly, told me in confidence-in the sense that I cannot attribute his remarks to him personally-that this kind of practice is commonplace. According to him, cases of money being obtained in advance from Government Departments ostensibly to make an immediate payment toward the total cost of a project, and then stashing the funds in a special trust account to earn interest for God knows who, are not at all rare. In many cases, according to this auditor, interest of that kind has been allowed to accumulate in special trust funds, ending up in the pockets of people who have no entitlement whatever
to that money. This money belongs to the taxpayers of Canada, so it should not be used in such a way. But when that kind of thing occurs, no one is the wiser. Certainly the Government does not know about it or, if it does, it does not care. The taxpayer is bilked millions of dollars each year through shoddy practices of that kind.
Crown corporations are, in effect, chunks of Government placed at arm's length from Parliament and Canada in a way that makes it virtually impossible for the elected representatives of the people to scrutinize their spending or operations. They have become empires unto themselves, controlling hundreds of millions of taxpayers' dollars with only the skimpiest of accountability to the Government and to the Parliament of Canada. As the CN Marine example demonstrates, the scope of Crown corporations for circumventing acceptable Government accounting procedures is almost boundless, as is their capacity to stonewall Government auditors once the corporations put their minds to it. And, ultimately, the taxpayers, whom those agencies are thereoreti-cally supposed to serve, end up paying the price.
The irony is that, having demonstrated its inability to manage effectively the taxpayers' money in connection with current Crown assets, CN Marine has set its sights on buying Northumberland Ferries Limited, a privately-owned company on Prince Edward Island that provides the only alternative ferry service to CN Marine's between the Island and the Mainland. That company was established in 1939 and operates four car ferries between Wood Islands, Prince Edward Island, and Caribou, Nova Scotia. Experts in the field consider the quality of its management exemplary, especially when contrasted to that of CN Marine. Yet here we have a Crown agency, CN Marine, making concerted efforts to buy out its competitor or, failing that, to seize its contract with the federal Department of Transport to operate the Prince Edward Island-Nova Scotia ferry service when that contract comes up for renewal in May, 1984.
Such a monopoly of car ferry service for CN Marine on the Island would be nothing less than catastrophic. It would be a tragedy for the Government, for CN Marine itself, and certainly for the people served by the car ferries in question. It would give the Crown corporation a stranglehold on the Province of Prince Edward Island, placing the company in a position to hike rates, slash services and dictate other conditions of operation without fear of restraint by market forces that only healthy competition can provide.
Moreover, a monopoly of that kind would render our Province terribly vulnerable in the event of labour strife, within CN. If such a monopoly had prevailed for example in the summer of 1973, when a Canada-wide CN strike shut down the Prince Edward Island-New Brunswick car ferry service, the consequences would have been disastrous for the local economy. Even as it was, despite the alternative service available from the Northumberland Ferries Ltd. at the time, when the CN Marine strike crippled the car ferry service operated by it between P.E.I. and New Brunswick, the Island suffered great losses, especially in the area of tourism. Think,
March 29, 1983

sir, what would have happened had we been totally cut off from the Mainland, as would have been the case had CN Marine operated the Northumberland ferries Ltd during the strike.
If I seem hard on CN, it is because I intend to be. I respect Crown corporations and especially the employees of CN. But what I do not respect is the fact that the corporate elite of Canadian National, operating from Montreal, have generally given Prince Edward Island and the Atlantic region as a whole a bad shake.
Prince Edward Island entered Confederation in 1873 largely to save its railway. P.E.I. came in because its railway was floundering and the Province thought that its joining Confederation would be the best avenue for saving the railway in perpetuity. Indeed, unlike any other Province that I know of, P.E.I. enjoys a constitutional commitment, written right into the Constitution of Canada, by the federal Government to provide a continuous link with the rest of the country by rail. Yet CN has chipped away at the Island railway with such persistence that in recent years we have found ourselves in the position of having practically nothing left worth saving. We have lost direct passenger service. We have lost important freight rail lines. We have lost any real on the spot capacity to maintain and repair rail cars and rail lines. We have lost the heart of the Carload Centre, the central operation for the administration of freight to, from and within the Province. We have lost CN Express services everywhere on the Island except Charlottetown. Finally, and most recently, the car ferry service has been drastically reduced, and we face the possibility of a monopoly which would altogether threaten the whole ferry system.
In Prince Edward Island, where highways cannot provide an alternative to rail for commercial purposes because the Island lacks the rockbed required to sustain heavy road traffic, we will soon be bereft of any transportation system worthy of the description. Clearly, CN has written us off and the federal Government is allowing Canadian National to do so. The federal Government is a ready accomplice in this scheme to strip the Island of what little remains of its railway system.
Established by the Government to forge a country out of a vast and thinly populated land, CN has long since, in my view, given up its public service mandate everywhere in the country

not just in P.E.I.-in favour of amassing huge profits, no matter what the cost to the public interest. In fact, in many parts of Canada, Canadian National is no longer interested in operating as a railway company, so preoccupied and obsessed is it with turning a fast buck in glamour industries such as gas and oil, in which it is investing heavily at the expense of traditional operations.
The recent formation of CN Exploration, Inc., an oil and gas subsidiary that has become an active participant in resource development out West, particularly in Saskatchewan, demonstrates where P.E.I. stands in the pecking order of Canadian National. My seatmate in the House of Commons, the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight), said it perfectly:
Borrowing Authority
Taxpayers' money funnelled into (CN) has made it one of the biggest transportation companies in Canada. Yet CN is forgetting its primary responsibility and is overspending and investing taxpayers' money in the oil industry.
Canadian National, like so many other Crown corporations, has become a monster virtually beyond the control of either the Government, of which it is nominally a part, or of Parliament, let alone the people of Canada which these corporations are supposed to serve. It is bad enough that those conglomerates are spending hundreds of millions of taxpayers' dollars without proper accountability, but many are now assuming what I can only describe as a life of their own, far removed from the purposes for which they were established in the first place.
Let me conclude by saying that, if someone in Parliament or someone in the public, or some accountant within the Government, wants to get a grip on uncontrolled Government spending, he need look no further than Canadian National's books for a place to begin. This is one Member of Parliament who would relish the opportunity to help him turn the first page.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on Bill C-143, and I would like this afternoon to take a somewhat different perspective on this Bill. We all know that $19 billion is an almost incomprehensible amount of money for most of us, and certainly for most Canadians, to grasp. We certainly are most concerned that this money will be spent productively and for types of expenditure that are going to help with the recovery of Canada's economy.
We would like to know, as my colleagues have already said, how this money will be used. We do not feel that the Government has given us a clear statement on this question. We would like a more specific breakdown of how this tremendous amount of money, which is to be borrowed at very high interest rates, will be spent, and in what specific areas.
I would assume, in this time of very high unemployment, that a good proportion of this amount of money will be spent for job creation. It is therefore to this particular area of expenditure that I would like to address my remarks this afternoon.
Furthermore, on this whole question of unemployment and measures to counteract unemployment, to create jobs and to get our economy rolling again, we have been asked again and again by the Government-let us see if they are serious or not-to make positive suggestions rather than just to criticize. So this afternoon this is what I propose to do.
We have over two million unemployed. There are many hidden unemployed people who are not shown in our statistics, such as the women in the home who have not been able to get into the work force. There are many who have been laid off through attrition are not registered on Unemployment Insurance rolls. There are 600,000 young people coming out of school. Many people have been on welfare for some time and others have just given up looking for work. The Government's token effort to deal with this situation is to put money into

March 29, 1983
Borrowing Authority
short-term make-work projects. They are spending millions of dollars in this area. There are not enough jobs created. But also these are not the kinds of projects that are making some impact on the whole question of how to use human resources more productively. Nor do they create permanent kinds of community services and community enterprises.
Today I would like to talk about an alternative employment proposal for which we would like to see money requested by this borrowing Bill C-143. I would like to encourage unemployed people and many workers who are facing lay-offs also to consider worker co-operatives, enterprises which are owned and operated by workers themselves. Third sector co-operative enterprises have not been encouraged in Canada. We feel that they should be considered for job creation. Some of the $19 billion that the Government is asking us to authorize by this Bill could certainly be spent on permanent kind of job creation that is working very well in certain countries in Europe.
In European countries, workers' co-ops are flourishing. Some of them are community kinds of co-operatives and selfhelp services. Others are building co-operatives to help extend housing. Many workers' co-ops are very sophisticated high-tech industries which include a good deal of research and development into new technologies.
I propose that the Government allocate some of the funds to be borrowed under Bill C-143 for research and also initial development of workers' co-operatives, as an alternative third sector way of helping to create jobs and deal with unemployment.
During this period of high unemployment, people are searching for alternatives that will use their skills and experience. People who have worked all of their lives, who have so much experience and capability, are beginning to feel very depressed because they have been chronically unemployed now many months. These people are sitting at home doing nothing while they have tremendous experience and capabilities that should be put to work.
One alternative employment strategy which has been given little attention in Canada is the development of these workers' co-ops. Workers' co-operatives may be small, community-based services or large industrial enterprises. The common characteristic, however, is that workers own the enterprise collectively and they all invest their labour in the enterprise. They hire a manager or manage their effort collectively. They have a democratic say in all policy decisions.
This past fall, Mr. Speaker, I joined with over 20 cooperators from across Canada to study workers' co-operatives in Britain, France and Spain. I would like to take the time to put some of our findings on the record because I think it is very relevant to Canada. We visit small community co-ops, particularly in Britain, such as print shops, restaurants that were run co-operatively by the workers, bicycle repair shops, adult education centres and feminist co-ops, as well as toured older, larger industrial co-ops, some of which have been in existence for 30, or more years. They were producing shoes, chemicals, glassworks and even Triumph motorcycles. These were large enterprises that had been owned and operated by workers for many years. In most communities there also were
building co-ops that use the skills of carpenters and tradespeople who were formerly unemployed to produce housing and also to undertake repairs and renovations, something which is very much needed in every community in Canada.
In England Co-operative Development Agencies in local municipalities receive Government grants to assist workers to form co-operatives, as well as to conduct feasibility studies and to learn successful business techniques. In Wales, a particularly interesting experiment was just beginning. Unemployment in that country, is very high since many of the major industries such as the coal mines have closed down. There was a desperate situation in which trade unions also were very much involved. The Wales Trade Union Council is assisting in promoting workers' co-ops, and these in turn become a trade union affiliate. So it is a co-operative effort between cooperators and trade unionists who are equally concerned with the plight of workers as well as developing a viable industry.
In France we found very modern, sophisticated, co-ops that were working successfully in the high technology field. But of major interest to co-operators was the co-operative developments in the Mondragon region of northern Spain, the Basque area of Spain. In that area there are 80 industrial workers' coops. They produce a very wide range of industrial products such as furniture, bicycles, auto parts, tools and computers, some of which are exported to Canada. These co-ops are supported by a major co-operative bank. Our credit unions in Canada should be helping in this way. They have a technical co-op college to train young people. The young people attend technical school for half a day and work in co-op factories the other half. Thus they are able to pay their own fees and expenses.
There is a very significant research and development component which helps to develop high technology products for export. To assist their network of co-operatives, they have coop insurance programs, and welfare services are available to all co-op members. There are child care centres so that workers, women in particular, are able to have an equal chance of employment. There are producer and consumer co-ops which complement each other. These co-operatives form a network that provides jobs for almost 22,000 workers in the Mondragon community. They are worker owners.
That there have been no business failures in workers' cooperatives since 1956 at which time they were started by Catholic priests to encourage more self-help development in the Basque area. There have been no failures in over 100 industrial firms during that period.
During a time of very high unemployment in Spain, where the recession is as bad if not worse than in Canada, in the Mondragon area where the workers' co-operatives are the base of activity, there has been less than 1 per cent unemployment. Their last resort is unemployment insurance. They try to find jobs for their workers. If workers are unemployed in one co-op they transfer them to sister or brother co-ops.
March 29, 1983

Co-op workers who own their own businesses have a strong commitment to their job. Studies bear this out. They have a strong commitment to the total operation. They do not work for someone else. They work for themselves. They work together for a productive and successful operation. In successful worker co-ops, profits are re-invested in the business. Workers do not take their profits home in their pockets right away. However, when they retire many of them have a considerable equity in the business.
Workers often contribute sweat equity labour during the initial stages of business development. Modern marketing and business practices are essential components of successful worker co-ops. Union membership provides a wider affiliation and mutual help between different co-operative endeavours, as well as ensures good working conditions and a concern with national and international issues affecting working people.
Workers' co-operatives are not a solution for replacing obsolete or unsuccessful businesses. We were warned about this over and over again. Like any private business or state-operated business, co-ops have to be run efficiently with adequate initial capital, and sound management. Friendly Government legislation is needed to assist co-ops in the same way as it does other small businesses.
Research studies of workers' co-ops have concluded that industrial democracy results in higher productivity than in either private or public-owned enterprises. If they are established on a sound basis, co-operatives can be a most successful and fulfilling experience for the worker members. We found tremendous enthusiasm among workers. We found that an investment or labour effort far beyond usual working hours was common in most of these co-op developments.
We would not oppose Bill C-143 quite as strenuously if we were sure that the Government would put some of the billions of dollars which it intends to borrow into developments that would help to solve some of our industrial problems and put Canadians back to work. I am seriously presenting workers' co-operatives as one alternative that I hope the Government and Opposition Parties will look into.
What can the federal Government do to promote additional successful co-operative enterprises? First, it should look at the model developed in the co-operative housing field. The experience there is very relevant. It would not appear to require massive Government expenditures. A revolving fund of capital could be used for start-up funds which could be recycled as the enterprise becomes viable. That would be one consideration.
Unlike the make-work projects we now have in our communities, which are very debilitating, workers' co-ops would not be short-term job creation. At present people are not being trained, getting into permanent jobs and becoming productive. An investment in workers' co-ops would be much more productive. It would not be a handout or welfare program, but an investment in developing human resources and viable enterprises.
There would need to be regional co-op resource centres in Canada, such as there are in England. Housing co-ops in Canada also have them. Training resources would be available
Borrowing Authority
to provide advice, research and public education. That would be a first step. Help with feasibility studies also would be needed. Regional co-op resource centres should be developed in co-operation with the labour union movement as well as with Government. Otherwise there would be a competitive situation. As in Wales, mutual help between union members would be the ideal.
Start-up funds would be most important to assist co-operative enterprises. In England workers often used their redundancy pay as their initial investment in co-op ownership. A pool of capital should be available to provide start-up funds and help initiate feasibility studies.
In most new co-operative ventures there is a period of development when it is not yet a viable business with a product that brings in income for wages. It would make sense, at least during the initial period, if co-op workers could continue receiving Unemployment Insurance benefits, as is done now in some job-creation programs. This would build toward a permanent salary from a viable co-op enterprise.
There should be Government support for co-operative enterprises, just as there is for small business. We learned that it is important that there also be a co-operative banking system which would provide favourable loan arrangements. Co-ops could help each other through a credit union type of membership. Eventually networks of workers' co-ops would be developed. There would be national and regional support organizations such as have developed in the co-op housing field.
Through this Bill the Government is asking for blanket approval to borrow $19 billion. This is a typical Liberal tactic. We would like to know on what this money will be spent. Canadians would also like to know. We would like to see some of it spent on productive investment in workers' co-operatives in order to assist improvement in our economy and put workers back to work. Workers want to contribute as productive human beings. This would be a practical investment rather than a handout. Canadians have a right to know where the moneys borrowed under this Bill will be spent. Because of our huge debt load, they want every cent spent wisely and productively to rebuild our economy. During this time of very tragic high unemployment, I can think of no wiser investment, than to invest in the development of viable, self-reliant co-operative enterprises which are owned and operated by workers themselves, which will employ essential expertise, and which will produce Canadian goods and services both for domestic use and also for export.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was fascinated by the remarks of the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) representing the New Democratic Party, and her proposal that some of the $19 billion of increased indebtedness, the borrowing Bill which we are now debating, Bill C-143, be used to fund workers' cooperatives. It is a fascinating theory. It is amazing that the New Democratic Party can always import ideas which have

March 29, 1983
Borrowing Authority
been rejected somewhere else, and then try to make them work here. If the Hon. Member would like to see how well those workers' co-operatives work, she should go to those countries where it has taken its purest form, and that is, behind the Iron Curtain. If she would take a look at the East Bloc countries she would see how well those workers' co-operatives function. As a matter of fact, before those co-operatives were in place, the Soviet Union was a food-exporting nation, and it was not long after the co-operatives were instituted in that country that the Soviet Union became consistently a food-importing nation. It is always crop failure or it is always the weather that does it to them, but somehow the workers' co-operatives have never been at fault.
The Hon. Member should visit East Germany and see the lineups of citizens of that country waiting to get into a consumers' store, wanting to buy consumer goods. At a shoe store, for example, the lineups go out on to the street when a new shipment of shoes comes into that store because they know that a month later there will be none, because the co-operative system, you see, works so well, according to the Hon. Member for Vancouver East. There is an absolute paucity, a barrenness of consumer products in these countries, and the consumer products of the West are used as currency in the East Bloc countries where those workers' co-operatives work so well.
She should also take a look at the People's Republic of China where, for the past 25 years or 30 years, the workers' co-operatives have been functioning so well that they are now being rejected and they are turning to what was called in the Soviet Union in 1927, "The new economic policy". Because the whole concept of workers' co-operatives worked so well, Mr. Speaker, they were running into such consumer goods shortages that they had to give the small-businessman a break. So they introduced the new economic policy. They called those short-term business people "NEP-men". Now, Mr. Speaker, in Mainland China, they have to do the same thing because there is continual shortages of goods in that country. They have to introduce somewhat of a market system there. The Hon. Member for the New Democratic Party now wants to take an idea which has failed all over the world, has been rejected all over the world, and wants to impose it on the Canadian people. That is the kind of service the NDP wants to perform.
We are now in the last day of debate regarding the borrowing authority, Mr. Speaker. We are in the last hours of this debate. But while we may be completing debate on it, the effects of this Bill are going to go on literally for decades, because, as other Hon. Members and myself have said continuously throughout this debate, we will be paying for this literally for generations. We, sitting here in this House, are not going to pay this bill. It will be our children's children who will pay this bill. That is the inequity that this system is forcing on us.
I would like to mention the latest development, Mr. Speaker. The Government has known this is the last day of debate and that within hours this House will approve the further indebtedness of the Government to the tune of $19 billion. The Government knows it will be able to pay its bills after Thursday, or on Thursday. It knows that it is going to happen, yet
the Government has sent out notices to the RCMP headquarters all over Canada saying that the RCMP officers are not going to be paid Thursday, obviously because the Government has no money, so it says. That, Mr. Speaker, is about as sleazy a trick as the Government can impose on the RCMP force. These are people who are working for us every day, doing their best to serve the Canadian people. The Government knows it will be able to pay them.

speechtext:
As the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) said, we are under time allocation because the Government has imposed that on us. It knows it is going to get this Bill passed today. Yet it has gone out with this ruse across Canada telling the RCMP that they are not going to be paid on Thursday. That is sleazy, Mr. Speaker. There is no other word for it but "sleazy".
What we are seeing here, as other Hon. Members have said, is the pattern of the Government. The pattern over the past 20 years has been to spend all of the cashflow which comes in during years of prosperity, to spend it as it comes in, and then, during years of hard times, to borrow. I suspect many of us have forgotten some of the spending programs which were carried on by this Government during times of prosperity. It occurs to me, first of all, how this runs counter to the pattern of behaviour of the citizens of Canada themselves. I believe you are aware, Mr. Speaker, that Canadian citizens, on a per capita basis, have more money in savings accounts than the citizens of any other industrialized nation. Canadians, by nature, by history and by tradition are savers. They put their money into accounts. They are not the kind of spenders which the Government itself is.
It seems to me it is because of the frontier pioneering education which Canadians over the years experienced that they have become a nation of savers. They realized out on the frontier, on the old homestead, that whereas there might be a good crop this year, even a bumper crop, next year there could be a famine, a drought, an early frost, late spring rains, a total crop failure, a grasshopper infestation, or rust. Just because there is a good crop this year does not mean that next year there will be that kind of surplus. So over the years the Canadian frontiersmen, the Canadian homesteaders, the farmers, learned to lay by during the years of prosperity so that when the years of famine came there would be something to tide them over. That is the Canadian experience which is just the opposite of that of the Government. Whereas the Government ought to lead the way and set the example, in Canada it is the people who set the example, which the Government refuses to follow. We have a Government which, in years of prosperity, when the tax dollars are flowing, spends money like a drunken sailor-and I should not impute that to sailors.
Ten or 15 years ago, the Government was encouraging the young people of Canada to tour Canada, "Forget about the cost. The Government will provide hostels. The Government
March 29, 1983

will provide bus service. The Government will look after you. If you want to leave home, go to a local welfare centre wherever you happen to hit town. There will be a cheque waiting for you there." In terms of social costs, we must stop and wonder how many families the Government helped to break up because it was so easy for a kid of 12, 14, 16 years of age to leave home, strike out on the road, pick up easy money at the welfare office and forget about his relationship with his parents.
We must not forget also that great noble experiment in Toronto 15 years ago called Rochdale. That community college was a sump hole of Government funds through, I believe, CMHC. It became a byword, not only of Government financial failure but of social irresponsibility. Young people were making a garrison out of that place. It was so tough in there that the police were afraid to go in. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) must remember those days. Those young people were getting unlimited funds, and their major skill was not in attending classes and taking a disciplined course of study because that was a college where you just sat and grooved. Do your own thing. You are not going to have any stricture or structure imposed on you because that would be confining and you would warp the personalities of these young people. You have to do your own thing in order that the personality blossoms. Well, it blossomed so much that those poor young people became society's rejects. Their major skill was not passing courses; it was filling out application forms for more money. That is the way the Government was spending money in those days, instead of setting some of it aside so when hard times came we would have some money in reserve. That seems to me to run counter to our traditions and history.
It also seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that deficit spending in the guise of helping the unemployed has also been an abysmal failure. You would think that if deficit spending to help the unemployment problem worked, we would now be drunk with success because the deficit has certainly been going up. I just want to read some statistics on how it has been going up. The spending forecast of November, 1981 was for $75,450 million. The deficit would be $10,490 million. By June of 1982, seven months later, the spending estimate had gone up by almost $3 billion to $78,100 million, and the deficit was now estimated at $19,550 million. By October, five months later, the spending estimate was $79,210 million, and the expected deficit was $23,550 million. In February, 1983, four months later, the spending estimate was $80,400 million and the expected deficit was $27,200 million. So from November, 1981, to February, 1983, a matter of 15 months, the spending estimate rose from $75,450 million to $80,400 million, $5 million more, and the estimated deficit rose from $10,490 million to $27,200 million, almost three times as much in a matter of 15 months.
I have two points, Mr. Speaker. The Government has done a miserable job of planning and estimating. It is just out of control. Secondly, if deficit spending were to be the solution for unemployment, we would have had all of our problems
Borrowing Authority
solved in the last 15 months because of the ballooning deficits we have before us. But then I have before me a news release from the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) dated March 28, 1980. He talks about the Employment Tax Credit Program and he says:
"This will be a temporary measure designed to ensure that an effective job creation program continues while an employment strategy is being prepared for early announcement in the House of Commons," Mr. Axworthy said.
He went on to say:
After a slow start the program developed quickly. It is estimated that, by the end of March, more than 46,000 agreements will have been signed with employers-agreements providing for the creation of more than 67,000 jobs.
The simple question, Mr. Speaker, is: where are they? Where is the massive success that the Minister predicted just two years ago to the day? He said this would be an interim measure, a temporary measure while employment strategy is being prepared for early announcement in the House of Commons. That was two years ago and the announcement has not been made yet. Was it the NEED program, which was announced last fall and which is another abysmal failure? I guess, Mr. Speaker, the truism is that there is nothing so sure about history but that we do not learn from history. It is time for the Government to reassess its approach. Spending simply is not going to do it. It had better get in tune with the business community of this country to make sure they have some confidence in the Government. Rest assured, Mr. Speaker, that when an announcement is made by this Government which the business community is waiting for, the second response of the business community is going to be: when are they going to change it? The over-riding attitude in the business community is that you cannot be sure any policies announced by this Government will be in place for any length of time. There is insecurity in the business community. They cannot plan, they cannot predict what is going to happen. They do not know whether the Government is a friend.
I trust that when the Government announces the date of the new budget, Mr. Speaker, and as they prepare this budget, they will not only bring some kind of financial relief but will begin to foster an air of stability and trust in the country so that the business community can do the kind of thing it needs to do if the Government expects it to invest the kinds of dollars it wants to. No businessman is going to invest dollars if he is afraid that he will lose them because of the insecure climate which has been promulgated by this Government.

speechtext:
Rather a comment, but if the Member chooses to take it as a question I would be quite agreeable to hearing his reflections on the comments I make.

March 29, 1983
Borrowing Authority
I was interested in the Hon. Member's opening remarks in which he so obviously misunderstood the basic thrust of what the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) was saying. I find it difficult to believe that the Member who said, "We must learn the lessons of history", which were almost his concluding remarks, should somehow fail to understand the difference in the concept of workers' co-operatives outlined in some complexity and detail by the Hon. Member for Vancouver East in her remarks which immediately preceded his. He fails to understand that that is different from the state-operated approach, the history of which in many parts of the world she decried. She suggested that worker co-operatives were a better solution to harnessing both individual initiative and the willingness of people to work co-operatively together with Government and the private sector in order to achieve economic growth. That is what she was suggesting. Nothing that I heard in her remarks could conceivably be misconstrued and, I am sure unintentionally, misinterpreted in the manner in which the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) did a few moments ago.
If the Hon. Member did not deliberately misconstrue them-and I do not think that is what he did-then I can only say that his comments are a product of that peculiar kind of Conservative mind that seems to follow a single track. It does not open itself and its thinking to other ways of organizing economic structures that have been experimented with both in the East and the West, for almost 50 years.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hold a copy of Bill C-143 in my hand. I maintain that this is more than an innocuous piece of paper; it is actually a mortgage document. It mortgages the future of the young people of this country for years and years, and probably for their children as well. Clause 2(4) reads as follows:
For greater certainty, any amount borrowed under this section may be borrowed in a currency other than that of Canada and may be repaid in the currency in which it was borrowed.
That adds insult to injury, Mr. Speaker. What is going to happen when the time comes to pay for this is that the Canadian dollar will probably have slipped. The money will be borrowed from countries which base their currency on the U.S. dollar, so we will be paying back the billions borrowed, plus interest, plus the exchange. It is even worse than it looks on the surface. Now, we all realize that income tax is the major method of extracting revenue from the Canadian people and that the squeeze is on.
My untimely departure from the House last week unfortunately prevented me from making several key points about the
nature of Section 31 of the Income Tax Act and the profound effect it is having upon farmers in this country. I want to bring that up in this debate because one of the reasons we are borrowing money is that the Government's planning is so inept that not only has it had to squeeze farmers but it is going to have to mortgage their children's future as well.
As I recall, prior to exposing the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) for what he was-and in my opinion still is-I was about to note the legal ramifications of Section 31 of the Income Tax Act. As I noted, it breaks farmers into three groups-full-time, part-time and hobby farmers. Revenue Canada has lately been reclassifying farmers for tax purposes from full-time to part-time and from part-time to the hobby classification. Our present definitions of these categories stem largely from the Muldowan v. The Queen case which reached the Supreme Court in 1977.
In Muldowan v. The Queen, the original Section of the Act was described by Mr. Justice Dickson as awkwardly worded and intractable. He pointed out some interesting anomalies in Section 31. The first question addressed by Justice Dickson was whether farming could constitute a source of income in a year in which a loss was suffered. He pointed out that the Section came into play only when the taxpayer had had a farming loss in the year. "That being so," he said, "it may seem strange that the Section should speak of farming as the taxpayer's chief source of income for the taxation year ..." In other words, how can you talk about using income to determine whether a farmer is a full-time, part-time, or hobby farmer when all three, under this Section, would be claiming losses.
The March 8 edition of the "Canadian Taxpayer" deals with this case in a very lucid manner. In an article entitled, "Why Not Kill Section 31?", this publication notes that Mr. Justice Dickson ruled that farming could constitute a source of income in a year when there was a loss as long as there was a reasonable expectation of profit. This reasonable expectation of profit has become a very important point in the classification of farmers under Section 31.
The second issue considered by Mr. Justice Dickson was the legal meaning of the word "combination" in the phrase "combination of farming and some other source". According to Section 31, a full-time farmer can have a part-time job off the farm and still retain his full-time status, and similarly a part-time farmer can have an off-farm job without being reclassified as a hobby farmer. Justice Dickson clarified these classifications as best he could. In his ruling he introduced the following classifications.
First, a taxpayer for whom farming may reasonably be expected to provide the bulk of income for his livelihood is free of the limitation of Section 13(1)-this is now Section 31 of the Act-in those years in which he sustained a farming loss.
The second classification is that of the taxpayer who does not look to farming, or to farming and some subordinate source of income for his livelihood, but carries on farming as a
March 29, 1983

sideline business. Such a taxpayer is entitled to the deductions spelled out in Section 13(1) in respect of farm losses, that is, $5,000 per year.
The third classification is that of the taxpayer who does not look to farming, or to farming and some subordinate source of income for his livelihood, and who carries on some farming activities as a hobby. This is the so-called hobby farmer. The losses sustained by such a taxpayer on his non-business are not deductible in any amount.
These classifications raise the question of whether we in fact need Section 31 at all. Once again, the "Canadian Taxpayer" deals with this matter in a very logical manner. The article
says:
The judgment, however, gives rise to the question of whether there is any need or justification for keeping the Section in the Act at all.
It does not apply to the first or third of His Lordship's classes of farmers. Taxpayers in the first class can claim their total losses like any other business people, while those in the third class cannot claim any deduction at all, because the Act specifically prohibits deduction of personal or living expenses.
That leaves the second class, but who is in it? Anyone who farms with a reasonable expectation of profit is 'farming', as the courts have confirmed. Where, then is the justification for restricting the loss such a person may claim as a deduction? In the Court of Appeal in the Muldowan case, Mr. Justice Pratte said that because of the Section "A limit is placed on the deductibility of commercial farming losses where farming is carried on as a subordinate activity, even though no such limit appears to have been placed on the deductibility of other types of subordinate commercial loss." Obviously the provision can be extremely unfair to some taxpayers.
As long ago as 1976 the Joint Committee of the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants and the Canadian Bar Association recommended to the then Minister of Revenue and the then Minister of Finance that Section 31 be repealed. The Government has failed to act on that advice. Instead, it has continued to tax farmers on a basis that is patently unfair and discriminatory. We must question the motives of the Government for keeping this Section of the Income Tax Act in existence.
The only rational explanation for the retention of Section 31 of the Income Tax Act is that it is a money-maker for the Government. It is a tax grab by a Government that is desperately trying to cover a mounting debt. Never mind that farmers are being forced into bankruptcy by this unfair rule. Never mind that no other commercial venture is subject to similar regulations. The Government does not care. Section 31 brings in revenue, and that is all that matters to a Government which is both financially and morally bankrupt.
I should like to refer to an editorial which appeared on March 15 in the Cariboo Observer, a prominent paper in my riding. It commented upon Section 31 under the heading, "Greedy Attacks". It reads:
Ranchers and farmers in the Cariboo are feeling the heat from relentless attacks by our provincial and federal Governments. The undisputed backbone of our nation, ranchers and farmers brought this wilderness out of the dark ages and into the twentieth century mainstream almost singlehandedly. It is tragic, under present economic conditions, that those ranchers and farmers trying to make ends meet, now find that that very activity which makes their operations viable is used against them by income tax investigators.
These internal revenue "revenooers"-call them what you want-are not interested in illicit whiskey distillers. They are out after tamer game: respectable,
Borrowing Authority
responsible, hard-working people trying to build a future with sweat, sacrifice and scarce dollars.
This is free enterprise? This is the land of endless opportunity?
No way. This is pure greed, displayed for all to see by a grasping group of civil servants, punishing people for trying harder.
There are choice words for this type of injustice. We can't print them.
One such person in my riding has been assessed four years of back taxes, amounting to $28,184.07, because he was classified as a part-time farmer. The man has put his heart and soul into his ranch since 1972 when he inherited it from his father. This individual is currently living with his wife and three young children on his land in the basement of an unfinished house. He cannot afford to finish the house. It currently does not even have running water. Yet the Department of National Revenue has determined that this man owes them $28,184. Where was the Minister of Agriculture, that great defender of the Canadian farmer, when my constituent was assessed these back taxes? The Minister of Agriculture wrote to me on this case when I referred to him for help. This is what he wrote:
Yours is one of a number of representations I have received on this issue, and I thank you for bringing to my attention these examples of the impact of present tax law.
That is the help we received from the Minister of Agriculture. I should have been named and removed from the House of Commons last week. However, I should have been named for understating the case against the Minister of Agriculture; that is why I should have been thrown out. The Minister says that the world is one big roast beef; the Minister is one big ham.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on third reading of Bill C-143. In effect, the Government has come before us and asked for approval to borrow $19 billion-$5 billion for this year and $14 billion for next year.
I should like to turn to the statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) on February 17, 1983, wherein he said that upon his appointment as Minister of Finance one of his basic tenets would be to inform the Canadian people fully of

March 29, 1983
Borrowing Authority
the economic situation as he saw it. He said that he had done this repeatedly and consistently since his appointment as Minister of Finance and that he would continue to do it in the future.
The Government's deficit in the coming year may be as high as $30 billion, yet we were told by officials in the Department of Finance-and this perhaps goes back one year-that they could judge six months ahead what would be the state of the economy and the borrowing requirements of the Government. Now we have a Government which comes before us almost weekly and tells us how much more it needs to borrow.
A couple of years back, in November 1981, the Government forecast a deficit of $10.4 billion. At that time we had real economic growth in the economy of 2.2 per cent. In June 1982, the deficit was $19.5 billion, with a real economic growth of minus 2 per cent. In October 1982, the Government projected a deficit of $23.5 billion, with a negative growth rate in the GNP of 4.4 per cent.
In the statement of the Minister of Finance of February 17, 1983, he suggested that the deficit would be approximately $27.2 billion, with a negative GNP growth of 4.8 per cent. One wonders how long we will have to put up with a Government that does not really know where it is going. Week after week it adjusts its figures on the deficit. Week after week it adjusts its figures on the borrowing requirements. In effect, it does not know which way it is going. Perhaps this reflects somewhat upon the business community because in reality businesses in Canada say that they cannot plan ahead. It is impossible to plan more than one year ahead in any business in Canada because one does not know what tax changes the Government will make.
The previous Minister of Finance, in the budget of June 1982, made what could be best described as a death-bed confession when he said:
Some say it should print more money. Others say it should let the deficit rip. But that would fail miserably. Inflation and unemployment would get worse. Interest rates would rise even more. Canada would price itself out of world markets. Recovery would be postponed.
If a deficit has been incurred as a consequence of measures to promote economic growth, there may be some economic benefits. At the same time, irrespective of how the deficit occurred, there are economic and financial costs.
There are two ways to Finance the deficit. One is by printing money. Over the past 12 years the Bank of Canada has financed $12 billion of the Government's cash requirements by monetizing its debts. Printing money leads to an expansion of the money supply, which may lead to an increase in the rate of inflation. The other method to finance the deficit is by borrowing money. In 1982, borrowing by the federal Government accounted for over 51 per cent of all new security issues placed in Canada. In 1983, the figure will be even higher. Borrowing of that magnitude clearly must have an effect on the supply and demand for money, and thus on interest rates which must be borne by the private sector. In effect, the Liberal Government has failed to exercise adequate cost controls. When one
examines the use of tax dollars, one sees that one out of every four dollars in tax revenue is used to service the public debt. That is an unbelievable figure. The total tax dollars spent to service the public debt is $16.7 billion. This works out to approximately $1,800 per taxpayer.
It is a fact that the Liberal Government cannot balance its books. Surely, if all businesses in Canada conducted their affairs like the Government, they all would have gone bankrupt. If a business does not balance its books, it cannot remain in business, nor would the Government allow it to stay in business unless it was a company like Maislin Transport to which the Government pumps in money to keep it afloat.
It is interesting to compare the Government's spending with the growth in the Gross National Product. The Liberals have maintained that the rate of Government spending will be less than the rate of growth in the GNP. In the year 1980-81, spending grew by 15.2 per cent while the GNP grew by 10.8 per cent. In the fiscal year 1981-82, Government spending grew by 16.7 per cent while the GNP grew by 13.2 per cent. In 1982-83, Government spending grew by 18.8 per cent and GNP grew by 5.3 per cent. In the projected year 1983-84, Government spending will grow by approximately 17 per cent and the GNP will grow by 8 per cent. The fact that the Government continues to increase its spending is incredible. Yet the Government attempts to maintain that it will not increase its spending. When will it adhere to policies that it sets down? The Government is devoid of ideas and does not follow through with any of its policies. Its policies only exist day by day.
Let us consider this from another perspective. Between the 1968-69 fiscal year and the 1982-83 fiscal year, federal Government spending increased by 624 per cent as compared to a 192 per cent increase in the Consumer Price Index for the same period. Since 1980, Government spending has increased by 68 per cent, while the Consumer Price Index during that same period grew by 37 per cent and the GNP grew by 33 per cent.
We have undergone two recessions since the Liberals came to power in 1980. The second recession began in the third quarter of 1981 and was exacerbated by the massive tax grab in the MacEachen budget of November, 1981. This recession has been the longest and most severe since the "Dirty Thirties". Canada's real GNP fell by 4.8 per cent in 1982. Since the second quarter of 1981, Canada's GNP has fallen by
7.5	per cent.
Businesses have suffered because of this decrease. Business bankruptcies were up by 33 per cent in 1982 as compared to 1981 and were 63 per cent higher than in 1980. Since August, 1981, there has been a net loss of 551,000 jobs. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate in February of this year was 12.5 per cent, not including the hundreds of thousands who have given up hope and have dropped out of the labour force.
March 29, 1983

One must also pause and consider the plight of those helpless students who will be coming on to the job market this summer only to be faced with the evident lack of jobs for them.
Other evidence of Government ineffectiveness can be seen in housing starts in Canada. In 1982 there were 126,000 housing starts in Canada, which is down from 178,000 in 1981 and far below the 210,000 units that CMHC has stated is necessary to stave off a housing shortage. This was due to extremely high interest rates and the poor state of the economy, all caused by the Liberal Government.
While it is true that we are experiencing a world-wide recession, it is also true that Liberal policies have made the recession far worse in Canada than it need be. One needs to look no further than the National Energy Program. The only explanation for the implementation of the national energy policy was the potential revenue that would have accrued to Alberta. It was never put in place to obtain self-sufficiency for Canada. Canada will not be self-sufficient by 1990. The National Energy Program was a short-term appeasement of the NDP and the other socialists on the Liberal side. They knew that if they did not act quickly, too much revenue would accrue to Alberta and they would not be able to stop that influx of money. Therefore, this program was a method to delay the large revenues that were accruing to the Alberta Government, the British Columbia Government and also to the companies.
It is interesting to reflect upon why the Government was unable to help Canadian companies, if that was its intention, through slowing down the increase in revenue to the foreign-owned companies. It is well known that the only companies in the oil industry to be hurt were the Canadian-owned companies. The foreign-owned companies were never hurt, nor was it intended that they be hurt. Elowever, through this policy the Government was able to buy some of these companies. It will be able to buy some of these companies at fire-sale prices.
Only the Canadian-owned companies have gone bankrupt or have lost massive amounts of revenue since only part of the revenue of foreign-owned companies is derived from Canada. Those companies do not have a problem. The other thing, of course, was that there was a massive amount of revenue from these companies leaving the country. Yet statistics have shown that 98 per cent of all the money that they received was retained and used back in the country. Therefore, the National Energy Program was only devised to appease the socialists who were in a hurry and those socialists who have lots of time.
Statistics Canada suggests that we will perhaps have an economic recovery in the next year. There has been some evidence to indicate that perhaps the recession is coming to an end. The major question now appears to be whether the positive evidence concerning consumer confidence and retail sales in the fourth quarter represents a beginning of the recovery in consumer demand.
Just as we need confidence in the business sector, so we need confidence in the consumer sector. If consumers are afraid to spend and do not do so, the retailer will not purchase goods.

That is the present state of the economy. Until confidence is restored in the consumer, the economy will not pick up.
In order to restore that confidence Canada needs stable policies instead of hearing the Government say every week that its deficit will increase. The situation will not improve as a result of the Government's introducing new tax policies. The tax law is complicated enough now. People no longer know how to fill out their income tax forms. Businesses spend up to 20 per cent of their time filling out Government tax forms. We cannot continue to go on like this if we intend to turn this economy around. We need stability in our economy. We do not need abrupt changes like the National Energy Program. We do not need abrupt changes like higher deficits that scare people and investors off.
A month and a half ago, I was in England with one of our committees. I visited a number of investment people in the City of London. I asked about the economic climate in a number of countries. I was told that the worst place for investing capital is North Korea, and next to that is Canada.

speechtext:
Speaking directly to the Bill, it is clear enough what the Government wants from Parliament with this Bill. It wants the authority to borrow $5 billion for the remainder of this fiscal year which, incidentally, ends in two days. There will be great amounts of spending in the last two days. As well, this Government wants another $14 billion for the next fiscal year. It is not clear, in spite of the best efforts of Members of the Opposition, on what the Government plans to spend this $14 billion.
We are being asked to approve this additional borrowing authority without even the benefit of a budget outlining the Government's spending priorities for next year. I understand this is the largest unbudgeted borrowing in Canadian history.
When I spoke on second reading of this Bill, I said my concern was with how the Government uses its deficit, not simply that one exists. Modern Governments have been using deficits as an instrument of economic policy for decades now. The Government should not be increasing the deficit in a reactive manner. It should not abandon its responsibility for guiding Canada's economic development, and resort only to deficit financing to cover its shortfall in tax revenues. No, the Government should be using the deficit to invest in economic recovery, to stimulate economic development that will increase Government tax revenues and, in the long run, reduce the need for deficit financing.
Instead the Government, in its last three budgets, has set its sights on cutting Government spending, hoping in turn to be able to reduce the deficit. But as we in the NDP warned the Government and the Tories with their new-found faith in the economic theories of the thirties, tightfisted fiscal and monetary policies brought on the recession that is now strangling the Canadian economy and causing the Government's deficit to skyrocket. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) himself has admitted that the increasing deficit is due in large part to the impact of the recession on Government revenues and expenditures.
It must be a bitter pill for the Government and its Conservative economic planners to swallow. In spite of their singleminded efforts to reduce Government spending and, hopefully,
reduce the deficit, the deficit has done just the opposite. The cost has been almost two million people out of work in Canada.
Let us look at past Government budgets just for a minute. In November, 1981, the Minister of Finance tried to speed up the pace of deficit reduction, setting his sights on a reduction from $13 billion to $10 billion in 1982-1983. But that did not happen at all. By the time he brought in the June, 1982 budget, the deficit was expected to be $19.6 billion. Now we are talking about a deficit for 1982-1983 of somewhere in the neighbourhood of $30 billion. That is three times what the Government had set its sights on barely 18 months ago.
It would be much better, I would say, Mr. Speaker, if the Government had had the foresight to bring in the kind of economic stimulation that would have blunted the impact of this recession; if it had chosen to invest its deficit in November, 1981, to speed up economic recovery, instead of sitting on its hands while the economy went into a tailspin, with the Government subsequently being forced to borrow billions of dollars to make up the shortfall in Government revenues caused by the recession. What the Canadian economy needs is not more Conservative economic quick fixes, but the kind of controls on Government spending that will ensure the economy picks up so that Canadians can benefit from Government expenditures.
I want to speak briefly about some expenditures related to my area as critic, namely that of the National Defence. The Tories love to minimize the importance of defence spending on the federal budget. Their constant cry is for more and more defence spending. We in this Party do understand that the Government must spend significant amounts of money in order to maintain an effective and modern defence force. But we do not believe that the answer to improving Canada's defence capabilities lies in throwing more and more money at it. It would make more sense for the Government to re-assess its defence priorities and then systematically set out the means by which it intends to meet those priorities. Currently Canada's number one defence priority is the surveillance of Canadian territory, waters and air space. Yet it is clear that successive Ministers of National Defence having ignored that priority in favour of training and equipping troops for their role in NATO. I agree with the Government that Canadian sovereignty must be our first defence priority, but it must be our first priority in deed, not just on paper.
I think this is very important when considering this borrowing authority Bill because defence spending consumes a great deal of the Government's operating and capital costs. Government spending on operating and capital costs, and by that I mean sending which excludes transfer payments, public debt and payments to certain Crown corporations, is estimated at $20.7 billion for 1983-1984. Almost 38 per cent of that spending, $7.84 billion, is consumed by National Defence. That is a pretty healthy chunk, and I think the people of this country have good reason to be concerned about how it is used.
March 29, 1983

For example, what possible value could it be to the Department of National Defence to purchase two Challenger executive jets with a price tag of $27.5 million?

speechtext:
I might be inclined to agree with you. It leaks, like the rest of the submarines.
Last year the total cost of the F-18 program increased by 26 per cent to more than $5 billion. I think it is more than appropriate to ask if our new "Star Wars" fighter, the F-18, is a good buy. I do not think it is. Why do we need the most advanced and the most temperamental new fighter planes to act as interceptors in policing our air sovereignty? A few years ago it was suggested that we might buy 50 used F-4 Phantom jets, refurbish them in Canadian factories and task them solely for Canadian air sovereignty missions. It was argued that the money saved could be used for such things as developing an ice breaking capability for our navy to do coastal surveillance and fisheries patrol. But that suggestion obviously did not wash with the Department of National Defence nor with the Liberal Cabinet, for that matter.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, there is another area of Government spending which I think Canadians should be very concerned about, and I am speaking about the Defence Industry Productivity Program. Government assistance to Canadian defence companies is estimated to be $169 million in 1983-1984, an increase of more than 190 per cent since 1979-1980. That is a pretty healthy boost in spending. It works out to a yearly increase of about 47 per cent for the last four years, for a Government which is supposedly committed to six and five.
I would hope that if the Government is prepared to increase spending on a program that much, it would make sure that it is getting good value for its money, but that does not appear to be the case. In the contracts for DIPP assistance, provisions are generally made for a repayment of the Crown contribution, once a reasonable and fair profit has been derived. But the Auditor General, in his 1981-1982 Report, said that there is no documented rationale for what is a fair and reasonable profit.
Borrowing Authority
So we have a situation where the Government has given out some $400 million over a four-year period but was only able to recover 6 per cent of that amount from completed projects.
Mr. Speaker, the Auditor General also slammed this program for its lack of documented industry strategies, for its lack of cost benefit analysis, and for the inconsistent monitoring of the use made by companies of money they receive from DIPP.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, let me reiterate that the Government does not need the kind of tight-fisted spending controls inspired by conservative economic theories that squeeze the life out of the Canadian economy. Instead, what is needed is a rational approach to Government spending and to the deficit so that the most value is obtained from Government spending and so that the deficit is not used only to react to the effects of the recession, but is used to invest in economic recovery.
