Mr. Speaker, I too am rising in the last 45 minutes before the bells will ring and we will be called forth and the Government Members opposite will stand once again and put the Government demand for more money.
As you know, we are standing here today under time closure on third reading. You will recall that, on second reading of the Bill when we discussed the principles of Government and the executive authority for borrowing this amount of money, time allocation was applied. It was closure. We were limited in our rights as Members on behalf of our constituents to object to this massive $19 billion borrowing Bill. After closure it went to a committee. The committee was effectively closed out by marathon sessions, lasting until 2 a.m. Yesterday, we had one day at report stage when we could ask questions. That, too, was under time limitation. We now have 45 minutes left at third reading on a Bill that will extract $19 billion from the Canadian public, $5 billion to get us over the next couple of days and $14 billion to get us into the new fiscal year.
This Bill is an affront to Parliament, an affront to each Member of Parliament, whether we sit on this side or the Government side. Members opposite would not in any instance get authority from their constituents to treat a borrowing authority Bill so cavalierly, but they will stand. Why? If they do not, they will be punished, as has been shown when Members opposite dared to stand for the rights of their constituents as compared to those of the monarch or king who sits with his appointed group of advisers.
They do not want Canadians to understand this Bill. I can understand that. It is an affront to every Canadian. Let us not forget our history. When this Government came to power in 1968 it was just following the days of Expo 67. We were a positive country with a health insurance and medicare system second to none in the world. We had a post-secondary education system that was turning out graduates who were young, excited and keen to get on with making this country work. Our economic system created ten jobs at least for every university graduate and jobs for all of the high school and community college graduates.
We had an Old Age Security system, Family Allowances and balanced budgets. The Government would come in with an expenditure program, followed by a budget that would raise every cent with no borrowing domestically or in the international marketplace. In spite of the fact we had come through the Depression and a world war in which 40,000 of our citizens died, we had a minuscule national debt. In short, when this Government came to power, we were a powerful nation with
the second highest standard of living in the world. We were charging up the mountain. It was an exciting place and we could hold our head high.
Then the Liberal Party went left. It made the mistake that so many absolute monarchs made so many times in history. We now have massive Government. The Government did it innocently. It offered all sorts of attractive programs. It agreed we should retain the small capitalist tax. The secret was, "Don't worry folks, we will borrow the difference". The Government said we were borrowing it from ourselves so there was nothing to worry about.
We had the benefit of the programs and a low income tax system. The Government was borrowing year after year. Government Members stood up and put the motions through, always on closure. Year after year Members on this side stood up and pointed out that while it may look good today, it will come back to haunt us. That is exactly what is happening today. It is true that chickens do come home to roost.
What are we faced with today? There is a lot of division among ourselves. There is an elected separatist Government in Quebec. A percentage of the voters in western Canada are committed to separation equal to the percentage that was in Quebec some 15 years ago. We have a national debt that is $200 billion, if you include the debt of the Crown corporations. We have a yearly deficit of $30 billion.
That means that over 30 per cent of all tax revenues go to pay the interest on the debt. We cannot create any programs with that money. It goes straight to those who already have wealth. As was discussed before, billions of dollars go to service that debt, concentrating wealth in the hands of people who already have wealth. That is leading to a class society, which is exactly what happened in Third World countries where there is a small percentage of people who have vast amounts of wealth and huge masses of people with no money at all.
That is what 15 years of Liberal Government is doing to this country, our mothers, fathers, sisters, brothers and children. It is something we would never do in our individual lives, yet somehow the Government has been able to convince us that it can do what we in our hearts know we cannot do at home.
Like every other country that has suffered massive Government intervention, we have had a devaluation of our dollar. It has gone down more than 20 per cent since these guys came into power. We all chuckled when France elected a socialist Government. Two years down the road now, it has massive debts. It has had three distinctive devaluations of its currency. I could have told you that the minute they were elected and tried to give people something for nothing, because it has happened time and time again. You simply cannot spend yourself to prosperity.
We are one half of 1 per cent of the world's population sitting on the resources of half a continent, and yet we are $200 billion in debt. It is absurd. Imagine what 24 million Japanese would do with this country. They are 114 million or 115 million people sitting on a rock in the middle of the ocean
March 29, 1983

with not one barrel of oil, yet their standard of living is much higher than ours. It is absolute absurdity, but it is the logical outflow of 15 years of the Liberal-NDP philosophy that Government can do things rather than people.
Fortunately, we still have those resources. The solution is a change of Government and to put back into place a Government that will create wealth by freeing up individuals from the restraints of Government. The combination of concentrating power in Ottawa, creating more and more Crown corporations and more and more regulatory agencies puts roadblocks in front of our entrepreneurs. Small-businessmen, such as those who set up and operate a fertilizer distribution service, a gas distribution service, a farmer, a small-businessman on the corner who starts with five or six employees and then 10, 15 or 20, is where the real economic wealth is created in this country.
The combination of regulatory agencies, municipal regulatory zoning bylaws all create so much red tape that these people simply give up. You then lose that momentum of growth and building. That is what happens when you get too much Government. The solution is simply, we simply have to cut it back.
The difference between the Liberal-NDP philosophy and ours is that they want decisions to be made by a small group, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), his Cabinet and a small group of economic planners. They want to make all the decisions on the capital of the nation, as compared with our philosophy, the philosophy that built this country, and indeed the western world. It was to take that absolute power that only the kings and queens had prior to the 1700s, split the capital of the country into millions and millions of individual pieces and let the individuals make the decisions as to how the capital should be allocated, used and renewed. Under that system, with millions and millions of individual decisions, men and women spent their whole lives on the allocation and operation of their small farms or businesses. That led to the generation of wealth to the point where the poor people in our country were better off than the kings and queens were prior to that time.
With increasing Government control and regulation since the war, we are now getting back the same problems people had before the 1700s. The ordinary citizen, the small farmer or small-businessman is essentially becoming a serf. Within 10 or 15 years, if we keep on with this philosophy, our farmers will be nothing more than serfs. We will be back to a form of feudalism.
I do not have to point out how badly off are our hospital insurance and medicare system. Our post-secondary education system is still turning out graduates. Because we have interfered with our economic system, we do not have ten jobs for every graduate today. In fact, we have ten students unemployed for each one who has a job. We have essentially reversed the formula and that, too, is simply a logical outflow of a small group of 40 or 50 people sitting here in Ottawa thinking that they can run this whole vast country. It has never occurred before, Mr. Speaker, and it will not happen in the future.

We are experiencing the result of huge deficits which lead to inflation just as surely as the sun comes up after the night, which in turn leads to the high interest rates, which in turn leads to a collapse. There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that it is a logical conclusion that this would happen because it has happened before. Is it an accident, Mr. Speaker, that even the Bible records that high interest rates are usurious? High interest rates became a sin because of the practical experience of the Jewish people who had been through this. It so affected them and so crushed the ordinary citizen, that the prophets picked it up, and it was put into their guiding book, the Bible, that it was wrong to have high interest rates. It is usury.
The Government seems surprised that we are in such trouble, Mr. Speaker. The New Democratic Party seems surprised. What is their solution? Their solution, Mr. Speaker, is more of the same, more Government. But we say, "Look. You have to break this cycle." They create the problems, and then their solution is more Government, which causes more problems, and what do they say? Let's have more Government. Why do they not try it the other way? If they looked at the United Kingdom today they would see that that country is truly starting to get its act together. For every year of a socialist Government, it will take at least two years of a Conservative Government to fix it up. Where would they rather live?
Something else which the NDP and the Liberals just cannot seem to get through their heads is again a lesson which comes to us from the Bible. All the great works from the past whether philosophic or economic, say that in the good years you put something aside for the bad years. Those Hon. Members deny the operation of the international marketplace, the invisible hand of Adam Smith. They simply wish to deny it exists, but it does exist. It exists whether you are a socialist country or a capitalist country. It is simply this: if you do not put something away in the good years, you will not have it for the bad years. Keynesian economics says that during bad times, such as a World War or the Depression of the 1930s, it is quite appropriate for us collectively to borrow money and to apply that to the creation of jobs. And it worked, Mr. Speaker, because the Government took only about 20 per cent or less of our GNP. Free enterprise was in trouble as a result of an adjustment phase which had to be made. Therefore, it worked. Then, during the good years, you must apply the other side of the coin, which is to pay the debt back, and the Liberals and NDP cannot escape from the criticism that during the 1970s, which were good years, instead of paying back the debt so we could be positioned in the 1980s to make the necessary adjustment to high technology, they took us further and further into debt.
We had balanced budgets in 1968. Now we have a $30-billion deficit. We had an absolutely minuscule national debt in 1968, during the good years, and we have taken that up to $200 billion. So that today, when collectively we in this House should be deciding that the Government needs to borrow $30 billion or $40 billion in order to take us into high technology,

in order to restructure our farming community and transportation in the West so we can get our products out, so that this tremendous industrial infrastructure in Ontario can be updated to employ our young people, we cannot do it.
Even the Government admits, Mr. Speaker, that once you reach $200 billion you are in trouble. When we had the programs and the low tax and Government was borrowing, some 5 per cent of tax revenue would go to service the debt, we would say that we thought that was too high. We would cut if off at probably 5 per cent. Government is cutting it off at 30 per cent. But what is the principle, Mr. Speaker? The Liberalism of today is not the Liberalism to which many of our parents and grandparents were attracted as the philosophy of a genuine reformist Party which was concerned about the individual. We no longer have the classical Liberalism. This Party is the classical Liberal Party which starts with the individual, then goes to the family. So it is no surprise to me that 15 years of the current Liberalism has led to four out of ten marriages failing. I am surprised that the six are still together. It is no surprise to me to see drug abuse, opting out and the suicides that are occurring today because they are a logical and absolute certainty in terms of the policies we have had and the view which the Liberal philosophy has of the state and the individual.
What a shame that our senior citizens are having to suffer as they are today. They felt they were building a future for themselves by paying into Canada Pension and putting their savings into RRSPs. They felt that when they retired at 65 with 2 per cent or 3 per cent inflation per year, by the time they were 80, sure, their dollar might be worth 50 per cent, but they could cope with that. They were proud and could hold their heads high. But as a result of the Liberal and NDP philosophy we have had inflation of 10 per cent, 15 per cent, and now the dollar has decreased in value in five years to 50 per cent. They are uncertain now. They do not have the future they should have. However, resources do not mean a thing, Mr. Speaker, unless you have the entrepreneurial spirit of people to go out and develop those resources and create jobs for our people. There is a solution, Mr. Speaker. The solution is to get rid of that Liberal Government and put in a Progressive Conservative Government.

I urge the Hon. Member to look at the facts and not the myths that have been presented. I ask him to look at a report which appeared in the Globe and Mail approximately a month and a half ago when Salomon Brothers, one of the important bond houses in the United States, indicated that the Canadian debt instruments are as valuable as the American ones. I suggest that before my colleagues opposite run our country down they should find out the facts to back up their allegations.
I was very interested in what the Hon. Member for Leth-bridge-Foothills had to say. He was able to recommend areas where we should spend millions and millions of dollars-on such things as youth employment, for example. He did not recognize that the Government has increased the allocation of funds for youth employment for this coming summer from
$120 million to $170 million. He wants even more. And he wants even more money to be spent on health care, although millions and millions of dollars are already spent there. Of course, these are worthy areas for spending and I will return to them.

He wants us to do these worthwhile things with one hand tied behind our backs. He brought out a bunch of the old Tory boogeymen. I think Government spending is helping to stimulate the economy in a time of great need. It is helping to maintain a vital safety net for thousands of Canadians who need it. It is replacing the vital private sector spending that will come about as recovery occurs.
As all of us admit, Mr. Speaker, borrowing is always a careful balancing act. If there was too little borrowing or too little Government spending, we would be plunged into new depths of recession. Let us be honest about that. If the Government were not involved in this spending program, if it were not practising an extra $25 billion worth of stimulation in the economy, we would sink even deeper into the depths of recession. That is a point that our critics have not conceded, however. They live in this "balancing the books" dreamland and forget that in tough times, debt and extra spending are legitimate tools for Government because they stimulate a sluggish economy.
We have said frankly and honestly to the Canadian people that too much debt and too much spending will re-inflate the economy and get in the way of the private sector recovery when it comes. We must constantly remind our friends in the NDP of that. I agree with the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills and the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) who want us to spend more money on human services. I cannot think of a politician who would want to see suffering or who would cut spending and ignore the results for individuals and their families. All of us feel that way, but the situation could be made worse for the people we are trying to help. We could stimulate inflation and high interest rates if we are not careful.
Borrowing is a balancing act. We cannot close our eyes to it completely the way some of the neanderthals and Reagan admirers want us to do. Equally, we cannot go hogwild and ignore our obligations and let the economy burn itself out.
We have tried to balance the act in two ways. We have watched the commonsense signals and not let the economy overheat. There are signs that our economy is recovering. In face of all the criticism that we are not doing things properly, that one fact stands out. The six and five program works; interest rates are coming down; inflation is coming down and jobs are being restored. These are the initial signs of recovery.
March 29, 1983

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Where?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
The Hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell) asks where. Apparently he has not gone back to his riding to see the numbers of people being rehired by General Motors in Oshawa. Despite his claims to be a friend of the auto industry he has not been to Oakville to see the rehiring there. The Hon. Member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) knows about it.
The economy is recovering despite the gloom and doom we hear from Hon. Members opposite. These are the common-sense signals I was talking about, and we have watched them to make sure that our behaviour was not creating gloom and doom.
The second thing we did is to reallocate money. We did that in June. We went through the six and five exercise to find honest ways to save hundreds of millions of dollars and reinvest it. We heard from our friends opposite when it was time to vote for that principle. The Tories voted in favour of the six and five program and the reallocation idea. They liked it, but when it came time for the specifics, to put it into practice, they voted against us. They voted against the reallocation which they say is so vital.

speakerposition: Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Louder.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
None of us are kidding in the House. We know that the Hon. Member for Burlington is busy shovelling away over there. He voted against cost cuts which were justified and legitimate, but we did not. We cut costs under the six and five program and put the money back into the economy in places where it was more badly needed. For example, we put it into housing. Thousands of housing units across the nation have been started with grants which we initiated and put forward to Canadian people. We found the way to restore that industry by reallocating money, by saving it from a place where it was not needed and spending it in a place where it was more badly needed.
That is the balancing act about which I am talking, not only watching the vital signals in the economy and watching the recovery, but also going constantly through our expenses and kicking out those that are not needed, kicking out those which do not have as high a priority, and bringing in ideas that are more useful today. This is what we have been doing with our borrowing and spending.
Also we have heard criticism that somehow we are condemning our grandchildren to eternal bondage to pay off the debts which we supposedly irresponsibly encouraged. It is better, according to this line of thought, that we should leave a blasted economy. It is better, according to the Tories who stand up so gleefully and preach gloom and doom, that we should do nothing and let the situation get worse. Now, would our grandchildren thank us for that? Would they be grateful if we left them with a blasted health care system, with a ruined education system, with no welfare and no unemployment insurance? Would they thank us for that? Those are the programs on which we are spending our money. We make no
Borrowing Authority
apologies for that. Those programs are not destroying the future of our grandchildren. They are preserving the vital safety net system which we have worked so hard to put in place. Why bother helping to build that network? My generation needs it and uses it as a right. We are passing it on intact to our grandchildren. We do not worry about that. In my own family, my father has been crippled for two years now by arthritis. He has said very clearly to me, "Do nothing about medicare, do not ruin medicare, or I will be a bankrupt man". We borrow money to finance medicare to help people like my father. I do not make any apologies for that kind of borrowing. It is responsible.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Let us put to rest this idea that we are destroying the country's future by the way we are spending today. We are not doing that. We are preserving the country in the face of enormous difficulty. The country wants us to do that. Let us go out into a public place-

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: All right, let us go.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
The Hon. Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) is willing. Let us go to his riding or mine and find out how many older people want their pensions cut the way he would do it, how many people want medicare cut the way his Party would do it, or how many want social services cut. Those are the implications of the program they are suggesting.
In conclusion I want to say that our spending has stimulated-

speakerposition: Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Your spending has stimulated unemployment.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: There are two million unemployed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
-our economy in a time of great need. Our spending has gone to the needs of ordinary people. Our spending has been constantly examined and reallocated. New priorities and new needs have been identified. Those are responsible acts by a responsible and humane Government.
